What I do 01 — 06

## AI implementation, *grounded in business reality.*

Most AI initiatives fail because they start with the technology instead of the process. I start with your P&L, your workflows and your constraints — then bring AI to where it actually moves the number.

**Direct answer.** Most engagements begin with the [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit) — a fixed-fee two-week sprint that produces a prioritised 90-day roadmap.

01 / STRATEGY

### AI Opportunity Audit

A structured diagnostic of your operations to find where AI delivers measurable ROI — and where it does not.

- Process & workflow mapping
- Use-case scoring by ROI and effort
- Build vs. buy vs. wait analysis
- Prioritised 90-day roadmap

[View package →](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit)

02 / BUILD

### Workflow Automation

Production-grade AI systems built on your existing stack — deployed, tested and handed over with documentation your team can maintain.

- Internal copilots and assistants

### Finance & Compliance AI

AI applied to the finance function by someone who has actually run it.

- Reconciliation and close automation

04 / ENABLE

### Team Enablement

Adoption is the real bottleneck. I train your people to use AI confidently and correctly, with guardrails that hold up under scrutiny.

- Executive and team workshops
- Prompt libraries and SOPs

- Ongoing advisory retainer

### Fractional AI Leadership

- Roadmap ownership and governance

How we work A — D

## From ambiguity *to shipped.*

A deliberately unglamorous four-stage engagement. No pilots that never leave the lab, no decks that gather dust.

STEP 01

### Diagnose

Two weeks inside your operations. I map workflows, interview your team and quantify where time and margin are leaking.

STEP 02

### Prioritise

Every candidate use case scored on business impact, implementation effort and risk. You get a ranked roadmap, not a wish list.

STEP 03

### Build

We ship the highest-value use case first, in weeks rather than quarters. Real system, real users, real measurement.

STEP 04

### Embed

Training, documentation and handover so the capability outlives the engagement. Optional retainer for the next horizon.

About

## Chartered Accountant. *AI practitioner.*

I’m Pratik Bajoria — a Chartered Accountant with over nine years of post-qualification experience across audit, financial analysis, taxation and business process transformation. Part of that career was spent at a Big-4 firm; the rest across industry roles and, latterly, building my own ventures.

The Big-4 years taught me something most AI consultants never learn: how enterprise processes actually behave under pressure. Materiality thresholds. Control environments. Why a workflow that looks inefficient on paper often exists for a very good reason. The years since — in operating roles and as a founder — taught me the other half: how to actually ship something inside a business that has limited budget and no patience for theory.

My advantage isn’t that I understand AI. Plenty of people do. It’s that I spent nearly a decade inside the finance and operations functions AI is meant to transform, so I can tell a genuine opportunity from an expensive distraction before you commit budget to it.

Today my main work is advising companies on AI implementation, alongside building **Findost**, my AI-powered wealth management platform. Everything I recommend to clients, I have shipped myself.

I also make a small number of [cross-border introductions](https://crossborder.pratikbajoria.com/) — connecting Indian businesses with international clients and buyers, and overseas companies with vetted Indian partners. Same lens, different problem: I vet both sides the way I would review a counterparty, and I am paid only if a deal closes.

# AI Opportunity Audit for finance teams and CA firms in India.

> AI opportunity audit by a chartered accountant: a fixed-fee two-week sprint that maps finance and CA-firm workflows, scores AI use cases and leaves a 90-day roadmap.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/audit
Last updated: 2026-10-26

Productised engagement · 2 weeks

An AI opportunity audit, run by a chartered accountant: a fixed-fee, two-week sprint that finds where AI moves your P&L — and where it does not. Mapping, scoring, build/buy/wait calls, and a prioritised 90-day roadmap. No vanity pilots.

**Direct answer.** An AI opportunity audit is a structured review of where AI can save time or reduce errors in your workflows, and where it should not be used. Mine is a fixed-fee, two-week sprint that maps workflows, scores use cases, and delivers a prioritised 90-day roadmap — so leaders know where AI moves the P&L before they fund a build.

For a CA-firm-specific explanation of the audit, read the [AI Opportunity Audit for CA firms guide](https://pratikbajoria.com/ai-opportunity-audit-for-ca-firms).

**2 weeks** Fixed sprint

**Fixed-fee** Quote on discovery call

**90-day** Prioritised roadmap

**CA-led** Ex-Big 4 · 9+ years

Fit check 01

## Who this is *for — and not.*

### For

- CFOs, COOs and operators who need a ranked list of AI bets, not a tool tour
- Finance and ops leaders under pressure to cut cycle time or error without adding headcount
- Founders who have tried “AI pilots” and want a P&L-grounded next step
- Teams ready to assign an owner and measure outcomes in 90 days

### Not for

- Shopping for a generic chatbot demo or slide deck
- Teams unwilling to share real workflows, volumes or constraints
- Engagements that need a multi-month strategy study before any decision
- Buyers looking for the cheapest tool recommendation without process ownership

Deliverables 02

## What’s *included.*

Everything you need to decide where to invest — and where to wait — without inventing a second programme of work.

01 / MAPPING

### Process & workflow mapping

Walk through the high-friction processes that actually burn time and margin. Document owners, systems, volumes and control points.

02 / SCORING

### Use-case scoring

Score candidates on business impact, implementation effort and risk — so “interesting” does not outrank “measurable”.

03 / DECISIONS

### Build / buy / wait

Clear recommendations per use case: build in-house, buy a tool, or wait until data, ownership or process maturity catches up.

04 / ROADMAP

### Prioritised 90-day roadmap

A sequenced plan for the first quarter: what ships first, who owns it, what “done” looks like in numbers.

How it works A — D

## Diagnose in *two weeks.*

The Audit is the Diagnose stage of the wider engagement model — compressed into a fixed sprint so you leave with decisions, not homework.

WEEK 1

### Map

Kick-off, stakeholder interviews and workflow walkthroughs. Surfaces where time and margin leak under real constraints.

WEEK 1–2

### Score

Candidate use cases scored on impact, effort and risk. Weak ideas are cut early — before they consume budget.

WEEK 2

### Decide

Build vs buy vs wait for each priority. Tooling only enters the conversation after the process decision is clear.

DAY 10–14

### Roadmap

Read-out with a prioritised 90-day plan, owners and measurement. Ready for implementation or a pause with eyes open.

Why a diagnostic first Why

## Fund the first win, *not the fifth pilot.*

Most leaders I speak to are not short of AI ideas. They are short of a defensible answer to a simpler question: which one should we fund first, and how will we know it worked? Without that answer, the default is a pilot chosen by whoever saw the best demo.

The numbers say that default is expensive. Gartner predicted that [at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-07-29-gartner-predicts-30-percent-of-generative-ai-projects-will-be-abandoned-after-proof-of-concept-by-end-of-2025), citing poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value. McKinsey’s 2026 global survey found that [only 37% of respondents attribute any EBIT impact to AI, a share unchanged from 2025](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai), even though nearly nine in ten use it regularly. Finance is no exception: Gartner’s 2025 survey found [59% of finance leaders using AI, but 91% reporting only low or moderate impact at first](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025).

The Audit exists to close that gap before money is committed. As a Chartered Accountant, I treat it the way I would treat any investment decision: baseline first, controls designed in, and a written reason to build, buy or wait.

Investment 03

## Fixed-fee. *Confirmed on the call.*

Pricing

### Fixed-fee two-week sprint — quote confirmed on the discovery call

Scope, access and sector complexity determine the fee. No invented day rates on this page. Book a short discovery call and you leave with a clear quote — or a polite no-fit.

Method

## How the AI opportunity audit *actually runs.*

This is the method in full, so you can judge it before we speak — or run a version yourself. The two-week sprint covers mapping and scoring; the roadmap it leaves takes you to a working release by day 90.

### From two-week audit to a 90-day roadmap

**Days 1–20: map the work.** Pick the five to eight recurring workflows that consume the most skilled time or create the most rework. For each, write five lines: input, decision, output, owner, and what “good” looks like today. In a CA practice this is usually research and first drafts, document extraction, reconciliations, reporting packs and routine client communication. In a finance team it is close, payables, collections and management reporting.

**Days 21–45: score and cut.** Score each workflow on value (hours, cycle time, error cost, cash timing), feasibility (data availability, system access, process stability) and control risk (confidentiality, regulatory exposure, whether an error reaches a client or a filing). Be ruthless. Anything that needs clean data you do not have goes to the “later” column. Anything that would put an unreviewed answer in front of a client goes to “redesign”.

**Days 46–70: design one release.** Take the top one — occasionally two — and design the thin version: which team, which data classes the tool may see, where the human approval gate sits, what is logged, and the metric you will review weekly. Write the stop conditions now, while nobody is emotionally invested.

**Days 71–90: run it beside the old process.** Two to four weeks with one team, reviewed weekly. The output of the audit is not the deck. It is a working release with evidence, or a clean “no” with reasons.

### The plan on one page

90-day AI opportunity audit: phases, outputs and decision gates

| Days | Work | Output | Decision gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–20 | Map five to eight recurring workflows: input, decision, output, owner, today’s “good” | Workflow maps and a rough baseline | Do we have owners and data for at least three workflows? |
| 21–45 | Score value, feasibility and control risk; cut weekly | Ranked shortlist, with a “later” and a “redesign” column | Which one workflow (occasionally two) goes forward? |
| 46–70 | Design the thin release: team, data classes, human gate, logging, metric, stop conditions | Release design and pilot charter | Is the control design acceptable to the partner, CFO or risk owner? |
| 71–90 | Run beside the old process with one team; weekly review of the exception log | Evidence against the baseline | Keep, change or stop, in writing |

### The scoring rubric

Score each workflow from 1 to 5 on each line. This is a framework for your own data, not benchmark data.

AI opportunity scoring rubric (score your own workflows)

| Dimension | What a 5 looks like | What a 1 looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value: hours | Many skilled hours every week across the team | A few hours a quarter |
| Value: error and cash | Errors are costly, or cash timing improves | Little cost to an error; no cash effect |
| Feasibility: data | Structured data you already hold and can access | Data is on paper, scattered or owned by a third party |
| Feasibility: process | Stable, written-down steps | Changes every month or lives in one person’s head |
| Control risk (reverse-scored) | Errors are caught inside the business before anyone relies on them | An unreviewed error could reach a client, a filing or a regulator |
| Ownership | A named manager wants it fixed and will run the release | Nobody’s job |

### How to spot audit theatre early

Three signals tell me an audit is drifting. First, the idea list keeps growing after week three; a healthy audit shrinks its list every week. Second, nobody has asked for a baseline — not a perfect cost model, just rough volume, hours by role and the errors people already complain about. Third, the recommendations name tools before they name owners. If a recommendation cannot say who will be accountable for the metric, it is a brochure, not a plan.

Audit theatre versus a useful audit

|   | Theatre | Useful |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting point | Workshops and a long idea list | Five to eight recurring workflows with owners |
| Baseline | None, or a vendor’s benchmark | Rough volume, hours by role and known error patterns from your own data |
| Idea list over time | Grows every week | Shrinks every week |
| Recommendations | Name tools and platforms | Name owners, metrics and controls first |
| Output | A closing deck | One working release with evidence, or a clean “no” with reasons |

### Governance anchors to use in India

You do not need a heavy framework, but you should be able to show that the audit considered risk in a recognised way. These are the ones I use, depending on the organisation:

- **Any organisation:** the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) (govern, map, measure, manage) as a neutral checklist.
- **Indian policy direction:** MeitY’s [India AI Governance Guidelines](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639) (November 2025), which take a principles-based approach built on existing laws.
- **Personal data:** the [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014), notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phased compliance timeline.
- **Regulated financial entities:** the RBI’s [FREE-AI committee report](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=61018) (August 2025), with 7 sutras and 26 recommendations across six pillars.
- **Audit firms:** NFRA’s [General Principles for Technology Adoption in Audit](https://nfra.gov.in/staff-series-on-technology-in-audit/) (July 2026), including validation of tools before live use.

Treat all of them as prompts. Your chart of accounts, staffing and auditor’s expectations are the real constraints.

### Deliverables checklist

- Workflow maps (five lines each) for every workflow reviewed.
- Baseline sheet: volume, hours by role, error patterns, with how each was measured.
- Scored and ranked list, including what was cut and why.
- One release design: team, data classes, human approval gate, logging, metric, stop conditions.
- Cost of the next 90 days, including review time and change management, not just licences.
- Control notes: data protection, who reviews what, and for CA firms, which outputs a signing professional must see.
- Evidence from the parallel run and a written keep, change or stop decision.

### Monday-morning checklist

- List no more than eight recurring workflows and write the five-line map for each.
- Collect a rough baseline: volume, hours by role, known error patterns.
- Score value, feasibility and control risk; cut the list every week.
- Design one thin release with owner, data classes, human gate and stop conditions.
- Judge the audit by the release it ships, not by the length of the deck.

### Frequently asked questions

### What is an AI opportunity audit?

A time-boxed review that maps an organisation’s recurring workflows, scores each on value, feasibility and control risk, and ends with one designed release run beside the existing process, rather than a list of ideas.

### How long does an AI opportunity audit take?

About 90 days if it includes a real parallel run: roughly 20 days to map workflows, 25 to score and cut, 25 to design one release and 20 to run it beside the old process.

### What should an AI audit report contain?

Workflow maps, a baseline, the scored and ranked list with what was cut, one release design with owner, metric and controls, the cost of the next 90 days and, after the parallel run, a written keep, change or stop decision.

### Which frameworks should an AI audit in India refer to?

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a neutral checklist, MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines, the DPDP Rules, 2025 for personal data, the RBI’s FREE-AI report for regulated financial entities and NFRA’s 2026 principles for audit firms.

### Is an AI audit worth it for a CA firm?

It is worth it when partners want a defensible answer about where AI pays back. For CA firms the audit should also record which outputs a signing professional must review, because AI does not change who is accountable.

FAQ 04

## Questions before *you book.*

### What is an AI Opportunity Audit?

An AI Opportunity Audit is a fixed-fee, two-week diagnostic that maps workflows, scores AI use cases on impact, effort and risk, and delivers a prioritised 90-day roadmap before a build is funded.

### What do you need from us?

Access to process owners, a shortlist of workflows under pressure, and honest volume/cycle-time context. You do not need a polished data lake — you need clarity on how work actually runs.

### Is this a tool selection exercise?

No. Tools come after process and ownership. The Audit decides whether to build, buy or wait — then names the next step.

### What happens after the two weeks?

You leave with a scored roadmap. Many clients continue into implementation or team enablement; some execute internally. Either path is fine if the prioritisation is clear.

### Can this stay remote?

Yes. Remote interviews and screen-shares work well. On-site days can be scoped when the process is heavily paper- or floor-based.

### How do I start?

Book a discovery call, or message on WhatsApp mentioning the Audit. Expect a reply within one business day.

**Direct answer.** The AI Opportunity Scorecard is a free checklist that helps CFOs and operators score process readiness, data quality, ROI, risk and ownership before committing budget to another AI pilot.

Rate each criterion 0–10. Total of 100. Below 50 usually means fix ownership and baselines first. 70+ is when a structured Audit earns its fee.

## Email to unlock.

You’ll also join **The AI Implementation Brief** — a weekly, unglamorous briefing on what actually ships. Unsubscribe anytime.

Why score first Why

## Ten minutes now, *not a wasted quarter.*

The scorecard exists because most AI proposals arrive with a tool attached and the hard questions missing. Who owns the workflow? What does it cost today? What data will the tool see, and who checks the output? If those answers are blank, the score will show it, and that is cheaper to learn now than after a renewal.

Those gaps are common. Gartner predicted that [at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-07-29-gartner-predicts-30-percent-of-generative-ai-projects-will-be-abandoned-after-proof-of-concept-by-end-of-2025), with unclear business value and weak risk controls among the reasons. Use is also running ahead of design: in Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, [75% of knowledge workers said they use generative AI at work, and 78% of those users bring their own tools](https://news.microsoft.com/source/2024/05/08/microsoft-and-linkedin-release-the-2024-work-trend-index-on-the-state-of-ai-at-work/). And McKinsey's 2025 survey found [only about a third of organisations have begun to scale AI](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai), even though most use it somewhere.

Score honestly. A low score on ownership or data is not a failure; it is the most useful result the checklist can give you.

# AI Automation in India: A Practical Hub for Business Owners

> AI automation in India for owners and operations heads: which workflows to automate first, DPDP and RBI considerations, human review and a 90-day plan.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/ai-automation-in-india
Last updated: 2026-10-22

AI automation · Updated 15 Oct 2026 · 7 min read

Where AI automation actually pays back for Indian businesses, what the DPDP Act and sector regulators expect, and how to run a first project without losing control of the work.

Most conversations I have about “AI automation in India” start with a tool and end with a pilot nobody uses. The businesses that get value tend to do it the other way round. They pick one workflow that already hurts, write down who owns it and what good looks like, and only then decide what to automate. I am a chartered accountant and worked at a Big 4 firm before founding Findost, so I come at this from the controls side: if you cannot explain the output to an auditor, a customer or a regulator, it is not ready.

This page is the index for everything I have written on automation outside the CA practice itself: sales and customer workflows, operations, governance and tooling. For the profession-specific guides, see [AI for chartered accountants in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india); for close, reconciliation and ROI, see [AI implementation for finance teams](https://pratikbajoria.com/ai-implementation-for-finance-teams).

## What AI automation should mean for an Indian business

Useful automation is narrow and checkable. In practice that usually means one of five jobs:

- **Enquiries and customer messages:** sorting and drafting first replies on WhatsApp and email, with a person approving anything that commits the business.
- **Documents:** pulling fields out of invoices, purchase orders, KYC files or property documents and flagging what is missing.
- **Reconciliations and exceptions:** matching marketplace, bank and ledger data and sending only the mismatches to a reviewer.
- **CRM and pipeline hygiene:** logging calls, updating stages and nudging follow-ups so the sales record reflects reality.
- **Recurring reporting:** first drafts of MIS commentary from controlled data, reviewed before anyone sees them.

What these have in common is a defined input, a repeatable transformation and an owner who can judge the result. That is also why finance is often the first function to move: Gartner’s 2025 survey found [59% of finance leaders using AI in their function](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025), up from 37% in 2023.

## By the numbers

The scale of the opportunity, and the size of the gap between using AI and getting a return from it. Each figure links to its source and date.

## Why so many automation pilots stall

The pattern is well documented. Gartner predicted that [at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-07-29-gartner-predicts-30-percent-of-generative-ai-projects-will-be-abandoned-after-proof-of-concept-by-end-of-2025), citing poor data quality, weak risk controls, rising costs and unclear business value. In my experience the fix is boring: a baseline taken before the tool arrives, a named owner, a review gate and a weekly metric. I have written that up as [the Monday morning test for any AI workflow](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-29-the-monday-morning-test-for-any-ai-workflow) and in [why most corporate AI pilots never reach production](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/corporate-ai-pilots).

## The Indian rules that shape the design

Two sets of rules come up in almost every Indian automation project.

- **Personal data:** the [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/02/Digital-Personal-Data-Protection-Act-2023.pdf) applies to digital personal data of individuals, and the government [notified the DPDP Rules on 14 November 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014). Customer chats, KYC files and employee data all count, so map what personal data each workflow uses before it reaches an AI tool.
- **Regulated entities:** if you are a bank, NBFC or other RBI-regulated entity, read the RBI’s [FREE-AI committee report (August 2025)](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/PublicationReportDetails.aspx?ID=1306). Even outside financial services it is a sensible checklist of what a regulator would expect to see written down: a board-approved policy, an inventory of AI uses and an incident process.

For a framework-neutral way to structure the risk work, the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) is free and practical. None of this is legal advice; confirm your position on your own facts.

AI adoption steps for Indian SMEs, drawn from the WEF, IndiaAI (MeitY) and PSA playbook for India’s SMEs (August 2025). Source: [WEF with IndiaAI and the Office of the PSA: Transforming Small Businesses, an AI Playbook for India’s SMEs](https://www.psa.gov.in/CMS/web/sites/default/files/publication/WEF_Transforming_Small_Businesses_2025.pdf).

### Text version of this infographic

- **Context:** India has more than 60 million MSMEs, contributing about 30% of GDP and about half of exports; only 19% of MSME credit demand is met through formal sources.
- **Step 1, find your data phase:** phase 0 is paper ledgers and manual logs (AI can look back at historical trends); phase 1 is spreadsheets, Tally, Zoho or a basic ERP or CRM (basic trends and automated reporting); phase 2 is APIs, sensors, QR tools and cloud platforms (predictive planning); phase 3 is fully integrated real-time systems (prescriptive, automated workflows).
- **Step 2, score each use case:** impact (business value, strategic alignment, people affected) and feasibility (operational readiness, cost to deploy).
- **Step 3:** start where impact is high and implementation is easy, then add use cases in phases. Microenterprises should begin with free or low-cost tools, AI-as-a-service and mobile apps; 85% of Indians have a mobile phone and 60% have internet access.

## A 90-day sequence that survives contact with the business

1. **Days 1–30:** pick one workflow, record today’s volumes, cycle time and error rate, and decide which steps must stay human.
2. **Days 31–60:** run the automation in parallel with the existing process, with every output reviewed and every exception logged.
3. **Days 61–90:** compare against the baseline and make a written go, adjust or stop decision. Only then widen the scope.

The full version, with an opportunity scoring method, is in [a 90-day AI opportunity audit without the theatre](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit). If you are weighing a custom build against an off-the-shelf tool, read [build vs buy AI tooling](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/build-vs-buy-ai-tooling) first.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is AI automation for a business in India?

It is using AI inside a defined workflow, such as reading an invoice, sorting a customer enquiry or flagging a reconciliation exception, so that the routine part runs faster while a named person still owns the result. It is different from simply giving staff a chatbot.

### Which business processes should an Indian company automate with AI first?

Start with work that is repetitive, has a clear input and output, and has an owner who can say what a correct result looks like: enquiry routing on WhatsApp or email, document extraction, reconciliation exceptions, CRM hygiene and recurring MIS drafts. Leave unsupervised advice and anything you cannot check for later.

### Does the DPDP Act affect AI automation?

Yes, if the workflow touches personal data of individuals in India. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025 set out duties on notice, consent, purpose, security safeguards and breach reporting. Map what personal data a workflow uses before you send it to any AI tool, and take legal advice on your facts.

### How long does a first AI automation project take?

Plan for one workflow over roughly 90 days: a baseline and design in the first month, a supervised parallel run in the second, and a written go, adjust or stop decision in the third. Scope it so it can be measured within a quarter.

# AI implementation for finance teams.

> Where CFOs and controllers should start with AI: month-end close, reconciliations, invoice intake and MIS, with controls, owners and a 90-day roadmap.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/ai-implementation-for-finance-teams
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Guide · CFOs & finance controllers

A direct path for CFOs and controllers who need measurable cycle-time and error-cost wins — without weakening controls, GST/TDS discipline or board-pack integrity.

**Direct answer.** Finance teams should start AI implementation on one high-friction owned workflow — close, reconciliation, invoice intake or MIS — map systems and control points, score use cases on impact and risk, then ship a prioritised 90-day roadmap with review gates. Tool demos come after process ownership. Prefer a free self-check via the [Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard), a structured [Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), or [book a discovery call](https://pratikbajoria.com/#contact).

Why finance first 01

## P&L pressure is already *measurable.*

Close days, reconciliation backlogs, invoice exceptions and MIS turnaround are numbers the CFO already watches. That makes finance a sharper starting point than open-ended “AI exploration”. The constraint is not models — it is ownership, audit trails and deciding what must stay human-signed.

01 / CLOSE

### Month-end pressure

Compress pack preparation and exception queues without removing controller sign-off on the numbers that go to the board.

02 / RECON

### Reconciliation & exceptions

Triage matches and mismatches with human review on material items — cycle time and error cost stay visible.

03 / INTAKE

### Invoice & vendor documents

Extract into ERP or AP flows with logging so GST/TDS and vendor master rules are respected.

04 / MIS

### Reporting with sources

Draft board and MIS packs from controlled sources; finance owns the narrative and the figures.

Fit check 02

## Who this helps *— and who it does not.*

### For

- CFOs and controllers who can name a process, owner and metric
- Finance teams under pressure to cut close or exception cycle time
- Leaders who want AI with review gates, not unsupervised postings
- Teams willing to share real volumes, ERP context and control constraints

### Not for

- Fully autonomous finance advice without human ownership
- Tool shopping without process or volume context
- Projects that need a multi-month strategy study before any decision
- Buyers seeking the cheapest chatbot list with no stop rule

How a CA-led, fixed-fee diagnostic finds where AI improves delivery and back-office throughput — without weakening professional judgement or client confidentiality.

# How to start AI implementation.

> How mid-market and finance teams should start AI implementation: map workflows, score use cases, then ship a prioritised 90-day roadmap — not another pilot.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/how-to-start-ai-implementation
Last updated: 2026-09-18

Guide · Mid-market & finance

A practical sequence for CFOs, COOs and operators who want measurable P&L impact — not another demo that dies in a slide deck.

**Direct answer.** Start by picking one high-friction workflow with clear owners and measurable pain, map it end to end, score candidate use cases on impact and risk, then decide build/buy/wait before you fund a tool. Compress that into a prioritised 90-day roadmap — the same discipline as an [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit).

Why most starts fail 01

## Tool-first is the *expensive default.*

Mid-market teams often begin with a vendor shortlist or a chatbot pilot. Without process ownership, volume context and a stop rule, pilots linger and never reach production. Finance teams feel this acutely: close, GST/TDS, reconciliation and MIS already have controls that AI must respect — not bypass.

01 / PRESSURE

### Choose a P&L pressure point

Month-end close, vendor reconciliation, invoice intake, exception queues or board reporting. If you cannot name the metric, you are not ready to automate.

02 / MAP

### Map the real workflow

Interview the people who run it. Capture systems, hand-offs, volumes and control points. Spreadsheets and email are part of the process — document them.

03 / SCORE

### Score before you buy

Rank use cases on business impact, effort and risk. Cut weak ideas early so “interesting” does not outrank “measurable”.

04 / DECIDE

### Build, buy or wait

Tooling enters only after process and ownership are clear. Waiting is a valid decision when data or governance is not ready.

Recommended sequence A — E

## Five steps that *actually ship.*

This is the Diagnose → Prioritise path compressed for leaders who need a Monday-morning plan.

STEP 1

### Pressure point

One workflow, one owner, one metric. Prefer finance and ops friction over open-ended research agents.

STEP 2

### Map

Walk the process with operators. Note volumes, cycle times, systems and where errors or rework concentrate.

STEP 3

### Score

Impact × effort × risk. Keep a shortlist of three or fewer for the first quarter.

STEP 4

### Decide

Build, buy or wait per use case. Assign an owner and a definition of done in numbers.

**Step 5 — Roadmap.** Sequence 90 days: what ships first, who owns it, how you measure, and when you stop. Many teams run this as a structured [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit); others execute internally once the prioritisation is clear.

Finance-specific 02

## Where finance teams *usually win first.*

### Strong first bets

- Reconciliation and exception handling with human review
- Document extraction into ERP or close packs
- MIS / board pack drafting with controlled sources
- Invoice and vendor-document intake with audit trails

### Usually wait

- Fully autonomous advice without review gates
- Broad “company chatbot” with no process owner
- Projects that need a multi-month strategy study before any decision
- Tool tours without volume or control context

Prefer a free self-check first? Use the [AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard). Ready for a structured two-week diagnostic? See the [Audit package](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit).

FAQ 03

## Questions mid-market *teams ask first.*

### Where should a mid-market finance team start with AI?

Start with one high-friction finance or ops workflow that already has owners and measurable pain — reconciliation, close, invoice processing or MIS — then map it before buying tools.

### Do we need a data lake before AI implementation?

No. You need clarity on how work actually runs: volumes, systems, hand-offs and controls. Many first wins sit on existing ERP, email and spreadsheet flows with light integration.

### What is an AI Opportunity Audit?

A fixed-fee two-week sprint that maps workflows, scores use cases, makes build/buy/wait decisions and delivers a prioritised 90-day roadmap. See the [Audit package](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit).

### How long before we see results?

A diagnostic can complete in two weeks. Implementation of the first ranked use case is typically planned inside a 90-day window with clear owners and metrics.

# Workflow automation with AI for mid-market.

> Workflow automation with AI for mid-market COOs: map hand-offs, pick owned bottlenecks, decide build, buy or wait, and ship automations within 90 days.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/workflow-automation-with-ai-for-mid-market
Last updated: 2026-09-18

Guide · Mid-market ops & COO

A practical playbook for COOs and ops leaders who need production automations on owned bottlenecks — not another pilot that dies in a slide deck.

**Direct answer.** Mid-market workflow automation with AI starts by picking one owned bottleneck with volume, mapping hand-offs and systems end to end, scoring build/buy/wait, then shipping inside a prioritised 90-day roadmap with a stop rule. Skip tool tours without process ownership. Next steps: free [Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard), structured [Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), or [contact](https://pratikbajoria.com/#contact).

Why pilots stall 01

## Automation without owners *does not ship.*

Mid-market ops teams often buy a platform or spin up a chatbot before naming the bottleneck. Without volumes, hand-offs and a stop/continue rule, work stays in “pilot”. AI helps when it compresses a real queue — documents, exceptions, routing, CRM/ERP updates — under an accountable owner.

01 / BOTTLENECK

### One owned queue

Lead qualification, document intake, order exceptions, support triage or internal reporting — pick one with a metric.

02 / MAP

### Hand-offs & systems

Walk the process with operators. Capture email, WhatsApp, spreadsheets, CRM and ERP as they actually run.

03 / DECIDE

### Build / buy / wait

Score impact, effort and risk. Tooling follows process clarity — waiting is valid when ownership is missing.

04 / SHIP

### 90-day production

Sequence what goes live first, who owns it, how you measure, and when you stop or expand.

Fit check 02

## Who this helps *— and who it does not.*

### For

- COOs and ops leads who can name a bottleneck, owner and volume
- Mid-market teams ready to ship production automations, not endless demos
- Leaders who want build/buy/wait clarity before funding another tool
- Organisations willing to change hand-offs, not only add software

### Not for

- Company-wide chatbots with no process owner
- Buyers seeking the cheapest automation list without metrics
- Engagements that need a multi-month strategy study before any decision
- Fully unsupervised customer or compliance decisions

INTAKE

### Documents

Extraction into CRM, ERP or packs with human review on exceptions and logging.

ROUTING

### WhatsApp & email

Triage and hand-off to the right owner without losing control of the conversation.

EXCEPTIONS

### Queues

Order, support or ops exceptions ranked by materiality so humans focus on what matters.

SYSTEMS

### Light integration

Updates to CRM/ERP and internal MIS once the process and ownership are clear.

FAQ 03

## Questions COOs *ask before funding.*

### What is workflow automation with AI for mid-market companies?

Using AI and integrations to reduce hand-offs, cycle time and rework on owned operational workflows — document intake, exception queues, WhatsApp/email routing, CRM or ERP updates — with clear owners and stop rules, not unsupervised company-wide chatbots.

### Where should a COO start?

Pick one bottleneck with volume and an owner: lead qualification, document processing, order exceptions, support triage or internal reporting. Map the real hand-offs before selecting tools.

### Build, buy or wait — how do we decide?

Score each use case on business impact, implementation effort and risk. Buy when a product fits the process; build when differentiation or integration depth matters; wait when data, ownership or governance is not ready.

# AI for AOC-4 and MGT-7 Filings: What a CA Can Automate Before the ROC Deadline

> How a CA firm can use AI to tie AOC-4 to signed accounts and build MGT-7 data before the section 137 and 92 deadlines, and what stays human.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-28-ai-for-aoc-4-and-mgt-7-filings-what-a-ca-can-automate-before-the-roc-deadline
Last updated: 2026-10-28

CA insights · 2026-10-28 · 6 min read

How a CA firm can use AI to tie AOC-4 to signed accounts and build MGT-7 data before the section 137 and 92 deadlines, and what stays human.

Key takeaways

- AOC-4 is due within thirty days of the AGM under section 137, and MGT-7 within sixty days under section 92(4).
- AI is best used to compare form data with the signed accounts and to build shareholding, director and meeting tables with a source on every row.
- Reasons for not holding an AGM, penalties, compounding, MGT-8 certification and the digital signature stay with people.
- Late annual returns attract ten thousand rupees plus one hundred rupees a day, capped at two lakh rupees for the company.
- Build the master data once for AOC-4 and reuse it for MGT-7, and keep client identifiers inside a firm-managed business AI account.

Late October is when the ROC season stops being theoretical. Most companies with a 31 March year-end held their AGMs by the end of September, which puts AOC-4 and MGT-7 on the same desk as tax audit follow-ups and the first GST notices of the half-year. Firms are now asking me a reasonable question: can AI take some of this load without putting a wrong number on a public record?

It can, if you are strict about where it sits. ROC filings are a good fit for AI because most of the work is carrying data that already exists from one document into another and checking that it matches. They are a bad fit for AI wherever the filing records a judgement or a certification. Below is how I draw that line, with the statutory dates the workflow has to respect.

## The dates the workflow is built around

Three sections of the Companies Act, 2013 set the clock, and every AI step below should be planned backwards from them.

- **The AGM.** Under [section 96](https://ca2013.com/annual-general-meeting/), an AGM after the first must be held within a period of six months from the close of the financial year (subject to the other conditions in the section and any extension granted).
- **Financial statements (AOC-4).** [Section 137](https://ca2013.com/137-copy-of-financial-statement-to-be-filed-with-registrar/) requires the adopted financial statements, with the attached documents, to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the AGM. Unadopted statements go in within the same thirty days and are taken on record as provisional.
- **Annual return (MGT-7 or MGT-7A).** [Section 92(4)](https://indiacode.ecourtsindia.com/companies-act/section/92/) gives sixty days from the AGM, or from the date it should have been held. Section 92(5) sets a penalty of ten thousand rupees for failure, plus one hundred rupees a day while it continues, capped at two lakh rupees for the company and fifty thousand rupees for an officer in default.

So for a company whose AGM was on 30 September, AOC-4 falls due at the end of October and MGT-7 about a month later. That gap matters. It means you can use AI for the AOC-4 tie-out now and reuse the same extracted master data for the annual return, instead of keying the shareholding and director details twice.

## Where AI earns its place in ROC work

The useful jobs are all variations of “read, extract, compare, list the differences”.

- **Tying the form to the signed accounts.** Give the tool the signed financial statements and the draft AOC-4 data and ask for a line-by-line comparison: every figure, with the page and note it came from. A person then checks only the mismatches and the figures the tool could not locate.
- **Building the master data once.** Shareholding pattern, transfers during the year, directors and KMP with appointment and cessation dates, meeting dates and attendance. These come from registers, minutes and earlier filings. AI is quick at pulling them into one table with a source reference against each row.
- **Cross-checking the board’s report.** [Section 134](https://ca2013.com/134-financial-statement-boards-report-etc/) lists what the board’s report must contain. A checklist run, with the tool marking each required matter as present, absent or unclear, is a fast first review before the partner reads it properly.
- **Year-on-year consistency.** Comparing this year’s draft against last year’s filed forms catches the dull errors: a changed CIN typo, a director still listed after resignation, a share count that does not roll forward.
- **The filing tracker.** For a firm with many companies, a tracker that reads AGM dates and computes the section 137 and section 92 deadlines, then flags anything missing, is the least glamorous and most valuable automation on this list. The arithmetic is simple; the value is that nobody has to remember.

## What stays with people

Anything that is a judgement, a declaration or a certification stays human, and the tool should not be allowed to fill it in “helpfully”.

- Whether the financial statements were adopted, and the treatment if they were not.
- The reasons statement where no AGM was held. That is the company’s explanation, not a template.
- Penalties, compounding and related-party disclosures in the annual return, which need the facts from management and the legal file.
- Certification. The annual return of a listed company, or one above the prescribed paid-up capital or turnover, must be certified by a company secretary in practice in MGT-8. The [ICSI guidance note on the annual return](https://www.icsi.edu/media/webmodules/publications/A29ChapterPages.pdf) sets the thresholds out as paid-up capital of ten crore rupees or turnover of fifty crore rupees. A certifying professional has to form their own view from the records; a model summary is not evidence.
- The digital signature. No workflow should store or apply a DSC on anyone’s behalf.

## A decision table for ROC filings

I use the same structure as the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework): map the task, decide the AI role, set the review gate and agree when to stop.

Evaluation framework only. Adapt it to your practice; this is not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Task | AI role | Minimum review gate | Stop if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deadline tracker from AGM dates | Automate | Manager checks AGM dates against minutes once | AGM dates taken from email rather than minutes |
| AOC-4 figures against signed accounts | Automate the comparison | Article clerk or senior clears every mismatch | Tool compares against an unsigned draft |
| Shareholding, directors and meetings table | Assist | Each row traced to a register or minute | Rows without a source reference |
| Board’s report checklist under section 134 | Assist | Partner reads the report in full | The checklist replaces the read |
| Reasons for not holding an AGM, penalties, compounding | Human only | Facts confirmed by management in writing | Any text drafted from a template without facts |
| MGT-8 certification | Human only | Practising CS forms an independent view | Certification relies on a model summary |

## Client data before the first upload

ROC files carry personal data: director PAN and DIN details, addresses and shareholder lists. Use a business AI plan whose retention and training terms a partner has actually read, mask identifiers the task does not need, and keep the extraction inside a firm-managed account. The same reasoning I set out for [DPDP and AI in CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric) applies here: decide your role on the engagement, then decide what the tool may see.

## Monday-morning checklist

- List every company whose AGM was held, and the date, from the minutes.
- Compute the section 137 and section 92 due dates and sort the list by the nearer one.
- Run the AOC-4 tie-out against signed accounts only; clear the mismatch list the same day.
- Build the master data table once, with a source against every row, and reuse it for MGT-7.
- Mark the human-only fields in each form before anyone opens the tool.
- Keep a short log: what the tool compared, what a person changed, who signed off.

If you want to see where this sits among the other workflows in a practice, start from the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india), or take the [free AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard) to see which compliance work is worth automating first.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI file AOC-4 or MGT-7 for a company?

AI can prepare and cross-check the data, for example by comparing AOC-4 figures with the signed financial statements and building the shareholding and director tables for MGT-7. The filing, declarations, certification and digital signature remain the responsibility of the company and its professionals.

### What is the due date for AOC-4 and MGT-7?

Under section 137 of the Companies Act, 2013, financial statements are filed within thirty days of the AGM. Under section 92(4), the annual return is filed within sixty days of the AGM, or of the date it should have been held. Check MCA circulars for any extension.

### What is the penalty for filing MGT-7 late?

Section 92(5) sets a penalty of ten thousand rupees, plus one hundred rupees for each day the failure continues, up to two lakh rupees for the company and fifty thousand rupees for an officer in default.

# AI Agents for Accounting in India: What to Let Them Do Unsupervised

> AI agents can now act inside accounting systems, not just answer questions. A CA’s rule of thumb for which tasks they may run alone and which need a human gate.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-27-ai-agents-for-accounting-in-india-what-to-let-them-do-unsupervised
Last updated: 2026-10-27

AI automation · 2026-10-27 · 4 min read

The vendor pitch has moved on from chatbots to agents: software that reads your books, decides what to do and then does it, whether that is posting an entry, chasing a customer or filing a reconciliation. Searches like “AI agent for bank reconciliation” and “AI agents for MSME” are growing, and the results are almost entirely product pages.

Agents can be genuinely useful in finance. But an agent that acts is a different risk from an assistant that drafts. This is the rule of thumb I use with clients to decide what an agent may do on its own.

## What makes an agent different

An assistant produces a draft that a person reads. An agent takes actions in a system: it creates records, sends messages, changes statuses. Regulators have noticed. India’s audit regulator, in its [July 2026 paper on technology in audit](https://nfra.gov.in/staff-series-on-technology-in-audit/), names agentic AI explicitly and gives an example of why validation should be proportionate: a translation aid and an agentic tool that selects and tests samples do not warrant the same scrutiny.

The same logic applies inside a company’s finance function. The more an agent can change, the more governance it needs before it goes live.

## A three-tier rule of thumb

- Tier 1, may run alone: read-only tasks and reversible preparation. Pulling statements, matching transactions, flagging anomalies, drafting reports and reminders into a review queue.
- Tier 2, runs with a human gate: actions that change records but can be reversed. Posting matched bank entries, updating customer status, sending standard reminders from an approved template. A person approves in batches, and every action is logged.
- Tier 3, never unsupervised: anything that moves money, files with a regulator, changes master data such as vendor bank details, or communicates a position to a client or authority.

## What the policy makers expect

Two Indian frameworks are useful here even though neither is a rulebook for a private company. The RBI’s [FREE-AI committee report](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=61018) for the financial sector sets out 7 sutras and 26 recommendations across six pillars, and MeitY’s [India AI Governance Guidelines](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639) take a principles-based approach that relies on existing laws. Both point in the same direction: board-level ownership, clear accountability, human oversight proportionate to risk, and the ability to explain and audit what a system did.

For a mid-market finance team, that translates into an owner for each agent, a written list of what it may do, logs you can read, and a way to switch it off.

## Bank reconciliation as a worked example

- The agent fetches the statement and the ledger, matches on amount, date and reference, and proposes entries for unmatched charges and interest (Tier 1).
- A person reviews the proposed entries in one batch each day and approves them; the agent posts and logs (Tier 2).
- The agent never creates or edits a payee, and never initiates a payment (Tier 3).
- Weekly, someone samples ten agent-posted entries and checks them against the bank statement.

## Do not skip the business case

Adoption of AI in finance has plateaued rather than exploded. [Gartner’s 2025 AI in Finance survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) found 59% of finance functions using AI, against 58% a year earlier. Agents will not change that on their own; a narrow, measured release will. Pick one process with a clear baseline, run it for a month, and decide on evidence. My [finance AI ROI rubric](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-12-finance-ai-roi-for-mid-market-companies-in-india-a-cas-decision-rubric) is a reasonable place to start.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is an AI agent in accounting?

Software that does not just answer questions but takes actions in finance systems, such as matching transactions, posting entries or sending reminders, based on rules and model judgements.

### Can an AI agent do bank reconciliation on its own?

It can fetch, match and propose entries on its own. Posting should go through a human approval step, and an agent should never create payees or initiate payments.

### Are there Indian rules on AI agents in finance?

There is no single rulebook for private companies. The RBI’s FREE-AI report and MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines set out principles such as accountability and proportionate human oversight, and NFRA’s 2026 paper covers agentic AI in audit.

### How do I decide which tasks an agent may run alone?

Allow read-only and reversible preparation, put a human gate on actions that change records, and keep anything that moves money, files with a regulator or changes master data under direct human control.

## Sources

- [RBI: Report of the Committee on the FREE-AI framework for the financial sector (press release, 13 August 2025)](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=61018)
- [PIB: MeitY unveils the India AI Governance Guidelines (5 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2186639)
- [Gartner: Finance AI adoption remains steady in 2025 (press release)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025)

# AI for Financial Due Diligence in India: A CA’s Decision Rubric

> Where AI helps in financial due diligence in India, from data-room triage to ledger analytics, and where a CA’s judgement, NDAs and SEBI UPSI rules stay in charge.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-26-ai-for-financial-due-diligence-in-india-a-cas-decision-rubric
Last updated: 2026-10-26

CA insights · 2026-10-26 · 7 min read

Where AI helps in financial due diligence in India, from data-room triage to ledger analytics, and where a CA’s judgement, NDAs and SEBI UPSI rules stay in charge.

Key takeaways

- AI can index the data room, scan ledgers, extract contract clauses, run reconciliations and draft narrative; each output is a list for a reviewer, not a conclusion.
- Quality-of-earnings adjustments, net debt, normalised working capital, tax exposures and the signed conclusions stay with the CA.
- Check the NDA before any upload, and use only business AI plans whose training and retention terms a partner has read.
- For a listed target, SEBI’s insider trading regulations require confidentiality agreements for UPSI shared in a transaction and a structured digital database with time stamps and audit trails.
- SEBI-regulated intermediaries are solely responsible for the output of AI tools they rely on, whether built or bought.

Financial due diligence is a CA assignment where someone else’s deal sets the deadline. The data room opens late, ledgers arrive in three formats, and the buyer wants a quality-of-earnings view before the term sheet goes stale. Firms increasingly ask me whether AI can read the data room, find the adjustments and draft the report.

My answer, as a chartered accountant with a Big 4 background who now builds AI workflows for finance teams, is that AI can take a real share of the reading and sorting. It cannot own the numbers that change the price. Below: where the line sits, the confidentiality rules that apply before any upload, and a rubric for deciding, task by task, what a tool may do.

## What AI is genuinely good at in a diligence file

Most diligence hours go into finding, sorting and reconciling, not concluding. That is where AI helps:

- **Data-room triage.** Indexing documents against the information request list and flagging what is missing, so gaps are chased in week one.
- **Ledger analytics.** Flagging large, unusual or round-sum entries and year-end reversals as candidates for normalisation, not conclusions.
- **Contract extraction.** Pulling change-of-control clauses, guarantees and termination rights from key agreements into one schedule.
- **Reconciliations.** Tying the trial balance to audited accounts and GST returns to revenue, with every difference listed for a person to explain.
- **First drafts.** Draft narrative and a running question list for management, from reviewed schedules.

Each produces a list for a person to work through: the tool narrows the haystack; the reviewer decides what is a needle.

## What must stay with the CA

Whatever moves the price or the sale and purchase agreement is judgement, and I would not delegate it:

- **Quality-of-earnings adjustments.** Whether an item is truly non-recurring depends on facts the ledger does not hold.
- **Net debt and debt-like items.** Deferred consideration, unpaid statutory dues and disputed liabilities need a view on substance, not a keyword match.
- **Normalised working capital and tax exposures.** Seasonality and pending GST or income-tax matters need management conversations and professional assessment.
- **The conclusions and the signature.** Whoever signs owns every number, including those a tool proposed.

The [NIST Generative AI Profile](https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence) names “confabulation”, confidently stated false content, as a core risk of generative AI. In diligence that is a plausible clause summary of a contract that says something else. Every extracted figure should trace to a page reference a reviewer has opened.

## Confidentiality comes before the first upload

Diligence information arrives under a non-disclosure agreement. Before choosing a tool, settle three questions.

**Does the NDA allow it?** Many NDAs limit disclosure to named advisers. Check whether a third-party AI service fits the permitted use; ask the counterparty if unclear. Use only business plans whose terms you have read; [OpenAI’s enterprise privacy page](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/) and [Microsoft’s Copilot privacy documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/microsoft-365-copilot-privacy) set out training, retention and access commitments for their business products. Consumer accounts are out.

**Is the target listed?** If so, much of what you see may be unpublished price sensitive information. Under the [SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015](https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/regulations/mar-2025/securities-and-exchange-board-of-india-prohibition-of-insider-trading-regulations-2015-last-amended-on-march-12-2025-_92672.html), regulation 3(3) allows UPSI to be shared for certain transactions, regulation 3(4) requires the parties to sign confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements, and regulation 3(5) requires a structured digital database recording who UPSI was shared with, maintained internally with time stamps and audit trails. Before any UPSI goes into an AI tool, ask counsel how the tool fits that framework.

**Is there personal data?** Payroll files, employee lists and promoter KYC are personal data under the [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf). Mask what the analysis does not need; my [DPDP Act and AI client-data rubric for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric) covers the steps.

If your firm is a SEBI-registered intermediary, such as a merchant banker, note that the [SEBI (Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/feb-2025/1739276753544.pdf) make a regulated person solely responsible for data privacy, for the output of AI tools it relies on and for legal compliance, whether the tool is built in-house or bought. SEBI’s [June 2025 consultation paper on responsible AI/ML usage](https://www.sebi.gov.in/reports-and-statistics/reports/jun-2025/consultation-paper-on-guidelines-for-responsible-usage-of-ai-ml-in-indian-securities-markets_94687.html) proposes model governance, testing and data privacy principles.

## A decision rubric for AI in financial due diligence

Before each engagement, agree the AI role, review gate and stop condition for every workstream. The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) organises this as govern, map, measure and manage; the rubric is the “map” step for a single deal.

Evaluation framework only. Adapt it to your engagement; this is not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Diligence workstream | AI role | Minimum review gate | Stop if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Data-room indexing and gap list | Automate | Associate checks the gap list against the request list | Tool cannot see all folders, or the NDA bars third-party processing |
| General ledger scan for unusual entries | Automate | Senior reviews every flagged entry before it becomes an adjustment | Ledger export incomplete or not tied to the trial balance |
| Contract clause extraction | Assist | Each clause checked against the page reference | Summaries without page references |
| Trial balance, GST and TDS reconciliations | Assist | Every difference explained by a person, with evidence | Differences closed by the tool without explanation |
| Quality-of-earnings adjustments | Human only; AI may list candidates | Engagement lead decides and documents each adjustment | Any adjustment proposed and accepted without management discussion |
| Net debt, debt-like items and working capital | Human only | Engagement lead and partner | Classification driven by keywords alone |
| Tax exposure assessment | Human only | Tax specialist assesses likelihood and amount | Exposure amounts taken from a model summary |
| Report narrative | Assist (first draft) | Partner reviews every number against schedules | Draft issued before schedules are final |
| UPSI or personal data of a listed target | Stop until cleared | Counsel and partner approve the approach for the deal | No confidentiality agreement or structured digital database entry |

What decides the role is how directly the output feeds the price and how sensitive the input is. Model quality is secondary.

## Where this fits in a CA practice

Diligence is a good place to prove AI value: heavy reading, fixed timetable. Run the first engagement in parallel with the usual process, as in the [90-day AI pilot playbook for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india), and apply the review gates in the [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india). The ledger-scanning approach overlaps with [AI for audit working papers](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-30-ai-for-audit-working-papers-in-india-what-a-ca-should-automate-and-what-must-stay-human); reuse what your audit team has validated.

For the wider map, start at the [AI for chartered accountants in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india) hub. To score your own opportunities, take the free [AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard), see the scoped [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), or [book a discovery call](https://pratikbajoria.com/#contact).

## Monday-morning checklist

- Pull your standard information request list and mark each line automate, assist or human only, using the rubric above.
- Read the NDA template you sign most often and note whether third-party processing by an AI service is permitted.
- Confirm the firm has a business plan for its AI tool, with training and retention terms filed by a partner.
- Write a one-line rule: no UPSI from a listed target goes into any tool until counsel has cleared the approach for that deal.
- Require a page reference against every figure a tool extracts, and spot-check them before review.
- Name the reviewer for quality-of-earnings, net debt and tax exposures on the next mandate.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI do financial due diligence in India?

AI can index the data room, scan ledgers, extract contract clauses, run reconciliations and draft narrative. Quality-of-earnings adjustments, net debt, tax exposures and the conclusions need a qualified professional who reviews the evidence and signs the report.

### Is it safe to upload data-room documents to ChatGPT or Copilot?

Only if the NDA permits it, the firm uses a business plan whose data terms have been read, personal data is masked and access is limited to the deal team. Consumer accounts should not be used for diligence files.

### Does SEBI regulate AI use in due diligence on listed companies?

The SEBI insider trading regulations govern how UPSI is shared, including confidentiality agreements and a structured digital database. SEBI-regulated intermediaries are also solely responsible for the output of AI tools they rely on. Take legal advice on the specific deal.

- [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Gazette text, MeitY)](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf)
- [OpenAI — Enterprise privacy](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)
- [Microsoft Learn — Data, privacy and security for Microsoft 365 Copilot](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/microsoft-365-copilot-privacy)

# AI for MSMEs in India: Three First Automations That Pay Back

> Where an Indian MSME should start with AI: three first automations in collections, bills and customer replies, with sourced context and the controls to keep.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-26-ai-for-msmes-in-india-three-first-automations-that-pay-back
Last updated: 2026-10-26

AI automation · 2026-10-26 · 4 min read

Most advice on “AI for MSMEs in India” is either a list of 20 tools or a national-level report about trillions of dollars of potential. Neither helps the owner of a ₹30 crore manufacturing unit or a 15-person distributor decide what to do on Monday.

I work with finance teams and business owners on exactly this question. My answer is to start with three automations that touch cash and customer time, measure them for a month, and only then think about anything bigger.

## First, be clear what kind of MSME you are

The category matters because readiness differs. The [RBI’s MSME FAQs](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/MICRO30072025E.pdf) set out the current definitions: micro up to ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover, small up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore, and medium up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore. The [AI playbook for India’s SMEs](https://www.psa.gov.in/CMS/web/sites/default/files/publication/WEF_Transforming_Small_Businesses_2025.pdf) from the World Economic Forum, IndiaAI and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser notes that microenterprises are more than 99% of MSMEs, often with paper records, and recommends they start with free or low-cost tools, mobile-based apps and AI-as-a-service rather than building anything.

Small and medium firms usually have an accounting system, a bank feed and a sales team. That is enough for the three automations below.

## Automation 1: collections follow-up

Pull the receivables ageing from the accounting system every week, have AI draft polite, specific reminders for each overdue customer, and let the owner or accounts head approve and send them. The draft includes invoice numbers, amounts and due dates, so the customer cannot claim confusion.

If your customers include larger companies buying from you as a micro or small enterprise, remember the law is on your side. [Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006](https://www.dcmsme.gov.in/msmed2006.pdf) caps the agreed payment period at 45 days from acceptance or deemed acceptance, and section 16 provides for compound interest on late payment. A reminder that cites the invoice date is often enough.

## Automation 2: supplier bills into the books

Bills arrive by email, WhatsApp and courier. AI tools can now read them, including photos and handwritten bills, and draft entries in the accounting system for review. The goal is not to remove the accountant; it is to have every bill entered within a day or two, so payables, GST credit and cash forecasts are current. The [AI automation in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/ai-automation-in-india) covers the review controls I would keep.

## Automation 3: first replies to customer enquiries

For many MSMEs the biggest leak is slow replies to enquiries on WhatsApp, email and the website. An AI assistant that drafts a first reply from your price list, product sheets and FAQs, for a person to approve, can cut response time without risking a wrong quote. Keep pricing, discounts and delivery commitments for a person to confirm.

## Get the data plumbing right

- Use one accounting system as the source of truth for customers, suppliers and balances.
- Prefer structured bank data to PDFs. Consent-based Account Aggregator feeds are maturing; [Sahamati](https://sahamati.org.in/media-article/account-aggregator-crosses-500-million-consents-as-india-marks-5th-aa-foundation-day/) reports more than 500 million consents on the network.
- Keep a simple log of what each automation did each week and what a person changed.
- Use business accounts for AI tools, not staff members’ personal logins.

## How to tell if it is working

Pick one number per automation before you start: debtor days or cash collected within terms for collections, days from bill receipt to entry for payables, and median first-reply time for enquiries. Measure for four weeks before and four weeks after. If the number does not move, change the process or stop. If it does, you have earned the right to look at bigger projects such as forecasting or inventory planning.

## Frequently asked questions

### Where should a small business in India start with AI?

With one or two automations that touch cash and customer time, such as collections reminders, supplier bill entry and first replies to enquiries, each measured against a single number for a month.

### Do microenterprises need expensive AI tools?

No. The WEF, IndiaAI and PSA playbook for India’s SMEs recommends microenterprises start with free or low-cost tools, mobile apps and AI-as-a-service models.

### What are the current MSME limits in India?

According to the RBI’s MSME FAQs, micro is up to ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover, small up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore, and medium up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore.

### Can AI help MSMEs get paid faster?

It can draft specific, timely reminders from the ageing report for a person to approve. Micro and small suppliers can also cite the 45-day limit in section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006.

## Sources

- [World Economic Forum with IndiaAI (MeitY) and the Office of the PSA: Transforming Small Businesses — An AI Playbook for India’s SMEs (August 2025)](https://www.psa.gov.in/CMS/web/sites/default/files/publication/WEF_Transforming_Small_Businesses_2025.pdf)
- [RBI: FAQs on Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (updated 29 July 2025)](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/MICRO30072025E.pdf)
- [Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (Gazette text, DC-MSME)](https://www.dcmsme.gov.in/msmed2006.pdf)
- [Sahamati: Account Aggregator crosses 500 million consents (2 September 2026)](https://sahamati.org.in/media-article/account-aggregator-crosses-500-million-consents-as-india-marks-5th-aa-foundation-day/)
