# AI Tools for Statutory Audit in India: What NFRA’s 2026 Principles Mean

> NFRA’s July 2026 principles on technology in audit, read by a practising CA: tool validation, scepticism, documentation and data duties for statutory auditors.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-23-ai-tools-for-statutory-audit-in-india-what-nfra-s-2026-principles-mean
Last updated: 2026-10-23

CA insights · 2026-10-23 · 4 min read

Search for “AI tools for statutory audit” and you will find a page of audit software vendors, each describing ledger scrutiny of every transaction and auto-drafted working papers. What you will rarely find is the regulator’s view. That changed in July 2026, when the National Financial Reporting Authority published the first paper in its Staff Series on Technology in Audit.

I have read it as someone who has signed off audit work and now helps firms adopt AI. Here is what it asks of auditors, and how I would turn it into a working policy for a CA firm choosing a tool.

## What the NFRA paper covers

The [NFRA paper, General Principles for Technology Adoption in Audit](https://nfra.gov.in/staff-series-on-technology-in-audit/), is principles-based and technology-neutral. It covers data analytics, automated tools and techniques, machine learning, generative AI and agentic AI, whether built in-house, licensed from a vendor or embedded in a network methodology. It is written for statutory auditors of public interest entities, but the principles restate obligations that already exist under the Standards on Auditing, so smaller firms would be wise to read it as a description of good practice.

Its ten principles include non-delegable auditor responsibility, applying the same evidence standard to tool output as to any other source, actively preserving professional scepticism, proportionate governance, explainability in line with materiality, and governance before deployment.

## Five points that change how a firm buys a tool

- The opinion belongs to the auditor. A tool can inform judgement but cannot be used to explain away a wrong conclusion.
- Tool output is evidence only after its relevance and reliability are evaluated, as SA 500 requires for any source.
- Fluent output invites automation bias. Reviewers must consciously challenge it, not just tick it.
- Validation should be proportionate: a translation aid and an agentic tool that selects and tests samples need different scrutiny.
- Tools must be validated and approved before use on a live engagement, not reviewed after the event.

## Questions to ask an audit software vendor

- Which procedures does the tool perform, and which does it only suggest?
- How are classification and anomaly rules defined, and can we see and change them?
- Is the output reproducible if we run the same data twice?
- What does the tool record for our working papers, and in what format can we export it?
- Where is client data stored and processed, who can access it, and is it used to train any model?
- How are product changes notified, so we can revalidate after material updates?

## Client data is still the firm’s responsibility

The NFRA paper is explicit that client and personal information must be protected in line with the firm’s confidentiality obligations and the [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf), and that a firm cannot rely on a vendor’s terms of service without validation. In practice this means a short due-diligence file for each tool: hosting location, access controls, retention, sub-processors and breach notification terms.

## Skills, not just software

The profession is building capacity quickly. At its [AI Innovation Summit 2026](https://www.icai.org/post/icai-ais2026-26062026), ICAI said it had trained over 50,000 members in AI and launched an advanced certification. That helps, but the NFRA principles point to a narrower skill every engagement team needs: the habit of asking how a tool reached an output before relying on it.

For working papers specifically, my guide to [AI for audit working papers in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-30-ai-for-audit-working-papers-in-india-what-a-ca-should-automate-and-what-must-stay-human) sets out what to automate and what must stay human, and the [CARO 2020 note](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-16-ai-for-caro-2020-reporting-where-it-helps-and-where-judgement-stays) applies the same thinking to reporting.

## A one-page tool policy for a CA firm

- An approved-tools register with the risk tier of each tool and its validation record.
- Rules for what each tier may be used for on an engagement.
- Documentation: what must be retained in the file when a tool’s output is relied on.
- Review: who challenges tool output and how that challenge is evidenced.
- Revalidation triggers: vendor updates, new data sources, or a change in how the tool is used.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does NFRA allow AI in statutory audits?

Yes. NFRA’s July 2026 paper neither mandates nor prohibits any tool. It sets principles: the auditor remains responsible, tool output must meet the usual evidence standard, and tools must be validated before use on live engagements.

### Do the NFRA principles apply to smaller CA firms?

The paper is addressed to statutory auditors of public interest entities, but it restates obligations already in the Standards on Auditing, so it is a useful benchmark for any firm.

### What should a firm check before buying AI audit software?

Which procedures the tool performs, how its rules work, whether output is reproducible, what it records for working papers, where data is stored and used, and how updates are notified for revalidation.

### What is automation bias in audit?

The tendency to accept fluent, plausible machine output with less challenge than a human-prepared equivalent. NFRA asks engagement teams and reviewers to counter it consciously.

## Sources

- [NFRA Staff Series on Technology in Audit 01: General Principles for Technology Adoption in Audit (July 2026)](https://nfra.gov.in/staff-series-on-technology-in-audit/)
- [ICAI: AI Innovation Summit 2026 press release (26 June 2026)](https://www.icai.org/post/icai-ais2026-26062026)
- [Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Gazette text, MeitY)](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf)

# AI for Tally Prime: Automating Data Entry Without Losing Control of the Books

> AI can now read bills and draft Tally Prime vouchers. Where it saves time, where errors creep in, and the review and GST checks a business should keep in place.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-22-ai-for-tally-prime-automating-data-entry-without-losing-control-of-the-books
Last updated: 2026-10-22

AI automation · 2026-10-22 · 4 min read

Tally is still the accounting system for a huge number of Indian businesses and CA clients, so it is no surprise that “AI for Tally Prime” and “AI for Tally entry” are rising searches. The results are crowded with add-on vendors, each promising one-click posting. Very few explain what should happen between the AI reading a bill and the voucher hitting the ledger.

I want to set out where AI-assisted entry in Tally helps, where it goes wrong, and the minimum controls I would expect before a business or a CA firm relies on it.

## What is now possible

Tally’s own [Docs by Ira](https://tallysolutions.com/tally/tallyprime-ai-invoice-processing-indian-smes/) reads invoices, including scanned PDFs, phone photos and handwritten bills, picks up GST fields such as GSTIN, HSN or SAC codes and tax splits, and drafts accounting-ready vouchers inside TallyPrime for review. Third-party tools do similar things for bank statements and bulk purchase imports. Vendors quote large time savings; treat those as claims to test on your own documents, not as a forecast.

This matches the broader finance picture. In [Gartner’s 2025 AI in Finance survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025), 59% of finance functions reported using AI, with document-heavy work such as payables among the common uses.

## Where errors creep in

- Ledger mapping: a new supplier, or one with two similar ledgers, gets posted to the wrong head.
- Tax treatment: intra-state versus inter-state, reverse charge and blocked credits are easy to get wrong from an image.
- Duplicates: the same bill arrives by email and WhatsApp and is posted twice.
- Dates and periods: invoices dated near month-end land in the wrong period.
- Capital versus revenue: an equipment purchase posted as an expense, or the reverse.

## The controls I would insist on

- Draft, then approve: AI creates vouchers in a review state; a named person approves before posting.
- Confidence thresholds: anything the tool marks uncertain, and every new party, goes to a manual queue.
- Duplicate check on supplier GSTIN, invoice number and amount before posting.
- Monthly reconciliation of purchase vouchers with GSTR-2B, because CBIC confirms in [Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-06/circular-cgst-193.pdf) that credit is available only to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B.
- A short exceptions log: what the tool got wrong and how the mapping was corrected.

## Do not stop at data entry

Faster entry is useful, but the bigger gains come from what clean, timely data enables. Payables ageing is one example. Under [section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006](https://www.dcmsme.gov.in/msmed2006.pdf), payment to micro and small suppliers cannot be delayed beyond 45 days from acceptance or deemed acceptance, and section 16 imposes compound interest on late payment. If bills are entered the day they arrive, an MSME ageing report becomes reliable enough to act on.

The same applies to month-end. Entry that is current means bank reconciliation and MIS can start on day one, not day ten. My [AI finance automation roadmap for CFOs and controllers](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-04-ai-finance-automation-roadmap-for-cfos-and-controllers) picks up from here.

## How to pilot it

Take one month of purchase bills for one entity. Run them through the tool while the team enters them as usual, then compare: ledger, tax split, period and amount for every voucher. Count the differences and the time taken on both sides. If the tool is right often enough that review is quicker than entry, extend it to a second entity. If not, you have lost a few hours rather than a quarter of clean books.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI do data entry in Tally Prime?

Yes. Tally’s Docs by Ira and several third-party tools read invoices and statements and draft vouchers. They should create entries for review rather than post straight to the books.

### What are the risks of AI posting entries in Tally?

Wrong ledger mapping, incorrect GST treatment, duplicate bills, period errors and capital-revenue misclassification. A draft-and-approve workflow and a monthly GSTR-2B reconciliation catch most of them.

### Do I still need GSTR-2B reconciliation if AI enters purchase bills?

Yes. CBIC Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST confirms that input tax credit is available only to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B, so purchase entries still need matching every month.

### How should a small business test an AI Tally tool?

Run one month of bills through the tool alongside normal entry, compare every voucher, and extend only if reviewing the AI drafts is clearly faster than entering them.

## Sources

- [Tally Solutions: How TallyPrime’s AI invoice processing (Docs by Ira) works for SMEs](https://tallysolutions.com/tally/tallyprime-ai-invoice-processing-indian-smes/)
- [CBIC Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST: ITC only up to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B from 1 January 2022 (section 16(2)(aa))](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-06/circular-cgst-193.pdf)
- [Gartner: Finance AI adoption remains steady in 2025 (press release)](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025)
- [Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 (Gazette text, DC-MSME)](https://www.dcmsme.gov.in/msmed2006.pdf)

# AI for ITR Filing: What a CA Should Let It Do and What Stays Human

> How a CA practice can use AI in ITR season: AIS tie-outs, document extraction and regime comparisons, with the review steps and data rules that stay human.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-21-ai-for-itr-filing-what-a-ca-should-let-it-do-and-what-stays-human
Last updated: 2026-10-21

CA insights · 2026-10-21 · 4 min read

Every July the same question comes up in practices: can AI take some of the ITR load off the team? The search results for “AI for ITR filing” are mostly vendor pages, and a few news pieces warning taxpayers not to trust a chatbot with their return. Both miss the practical middle ground a CA firm actually operates in.

This is how I would split the work: what AI does well in return preparation, what it should never decide, and the controls that make the speed safe.

## Start with the statement the department already has

The Annual Information Statement is where most mismatches begin. The department’s [Form No. 168 FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs) describe the AIS under the new law, and the [Income-tax Act, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2248005) came into force on 1 April 2026, so terminology and form references are shifting this year. That is a reason to be careful with any AI tool trained on older material.

Used well, AI is excellent at the tie-out: reading the AIS, the client’s Form 16, bank interest certificates and broker statements, and listing every item that appears in one place but not the other. That list is where a preparer’s time should go.

## Tasks AI handles well in ITR season

- Extracting figures from Form 16, interest certificates, capital gains statements and rent receipts into a standard working sheet.
- Reconciling the extracted figures with the AIS and flagging differences by category and amount.
- Running a first comparison of the old and new regimes from the working sheet, for the reviewer to confirm.
- Drafting the client query list: missing documents, unexplained credits, foreign assets questions.
- Producing a plain-English summary of the computation for the client email.

## What must stay with the CA

Form selection depends on residential status, the nature of income, directorships, unlisted shares and foreign assets. The e-Filing portal’s [guide to which ITR applies](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/help/individual/return-applicable-1) shows how many conditions are involved; an AI tool can suggest a form, but the preparer must confirm it from the facts.

Classification and positions are the other half. Whether a receipt is business income or capital gains, whether an exemption applies, how a loss is set off: these are judgements. As tax experts told [CNBC-TV18](https://www.cnbctv18.com/personal-finance/chatgpt-and-itr-filing-income-tax-return-what-ai-can-do-what-not-19949597.htm), using AI does not shift responsibility for what is reported, and an AI answer is no defence if a return is questioned.

## A workflow for a practice

- Collect documents through a firm-controlled portal or shared drive, not personal WhatsApp.
- Run extraction and AIS reconciliation in an approved tool; save the output to the client file.
- Preparer reviews every difference and records how each was resolved.
- Reviewer confirms the form, regime choice, any exemptions claimed and the final computation.
- Client approves the computation before filing and e-verifies the return.

## Client data rules

ITR documents are dense with personal data: PAN, Aadhaar-linked details, bank accounts, salaries and family information. The [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) were notified in November 2025 with a phased timeline. Decide now which AI accounts may receive client files, switch off training on your data, set retention, and never paste a client’s documents into a personal chatbot account. My [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india) covers the policy side.

## Measuring whether it helped

Track three numbers through the season: hours per return by complexity band, the number of AIS differences found before filing, and post-filing corrections or notices. If hours fall but corrections rise, the tool is moving work downstream rather than removing it. That is the same discipline I apply to [TDS reconciliation](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-13-using-ai-for-tds-reconciliation-in-indian-ca-firms-from-26as-to-form-168).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI file my income tax return?

AI tools can extract figures, reconcile them with the AIS and draft a computation, but form selection, classification and positions remain the preparer’s judgement, and the taxpayer remains responsible for what is reported.

### Is ChatGPT reliable for ITR filing?

It is useful for explaining concepts and drafting client communication. It may rely on outdated rules, especially with the Income-tax Act, 2025 in force from 1 April 2026, so every figure and provision must be checked against official sources.

### What is the best use of AI in ITR season for a CA firm?

Document extraction and reconciliation with the Annual Information Statement, followed by a reviewer-led check of every difference before filing.

### Is it safe to upload Form 16 and AIS to an AI tool?

Only to a firm-approved business account with training on your data switched off and retention settings checked. Personal chatbot accounts should not receive client tax documents.

## Sources

- [Income Tax Department: Form No. 168 (Annual Information Statement) FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs)
- [PIB: Income-tax Act, 2025 comes into force from 1 April 2026](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2248005)
- [Income Tax Department e-Filing portal: which ITR form applies to an individual](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/help/individual/return-applicable-1)
- [CNBC-TV18: ChatGPT and your ITR — what AI can do and what it may get wrong](https://www.cnbctv18.com/personal-finance/chatgpt-and-itr-filing-income-tax-return-what-ai-can-do-what-not-19949597.htm)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)

# AI for CMA Data and Bank Loan Project Reports: A CA’s Review Checklist

> AI tools now promise CMA data in minutes. What a CA should still check before a projection goes to the bank: turnover method, ratios, assumptions and evidence.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-20-ai-for-cma-data-and-bank-loan-project-reports-a-ca-s-review-checklist
Last updated: 2026-10-20

CA insights · 2026-10-20 · 4 min read

Search for “AI tool for CMA data preparation” and almost every result is a software landing page promising a bank-ready CMA report in minutes, often with a line about saving the CA’s fee. I have no quarrel with faster spreadsheets. My concern is what gets lost: CMA data is a set of forward-looking claims that a banker will hold the borrower to, and sometimes the CA who prepared them.

Here is how I would use AI in CMA and project report work for MSME clients, and the review checklist I would keep regardless of which tool builds the first draft.

## Why this work matters more than it looks

Formal credit is still hard for small businesses to get. The [AI playbook for India’s SMEs](https://www.psa.gov.in/CMS/web/sites/default/files/publication/WEF_Transforming_Small_Businesses_2025.pdf), published by the World Economic Forum with IndiaAI and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser in August 2025, says only 19% of MSME credit demand in India is met through formal sources, and that informal lenders typically charge 12 to 16% more. A well-prepared, credible loan file is one of the most practical things a CA can do for a client.

That is also why speed alone is the wrong goal. A projection that is quick but unsupported can get a proposal rejected, or worse, sanctioned on numbers the business cannot meet.

## Know which assessment method the bank will apply

The [RBI’s MSME FAQs](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/MICRO30072025E.pdf) note that banks must appraise genuine working capital needs keeping the business cycle in mind, and that under the Nayak Committee approach, working capital limits for small units are computed at a minimum of 20% of estimated turnover for credit limits up to ₹5 crore. The same FAQs state that banks are mandated not to take collateral security for loans up to ₹10 lakh to units in the MSE sector.

An AI tool will happily compute both the turnover method and the traditional MPBF approach. Your job is to know which one the lender will use for this client and to make sure the projected turnover behind it is defensible.

## Where AI genuinely helps

- Extracting audited financials from PDFs into the operating statement and balance sheet formats, with a reconciliation back to the signed accounts.
- Rolling forward projections from a short list of stated assumptions, and recalculating every form when one assumption changes.
- Computing ratios consistently (current ratio, DSCR, debt-equity, holding periods) and flagging the ones that look out of line with the sector or with history.
- Drafting the narrative sections of a project report from your notes: business background, the purpose of the loan and the repayment logic.
- Preparing a list of questions the banker is likely to ask, so the client can gather evidence before the meeting.

## The CA’s review checklist

- Tie the historical columns to the audited financial statements and the filed GST returns, line by line.
- Write down every projection assumption (growth, margins, debtor and creditor days, capex timing) and the evidence for it: order book, contracts, capacity, past trend.
- Check that projected receivable and inventory days are consistent with what the business has actually achieved, not what the tool defaults to.
- Recalculate DSCR yourself for at least one year and compare it with the tool’s figure.
- Confirm the client’s MSME classification. The [Union Budget 2025-26](https://pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2098389) raised the investment and turnover limits by 2.5 and 2 times, so older Udyam data may be out of date.
- Read the generated narrative as the banker would. Remove any sentence the client cannot evidence.

## Red flags in AI-generated projections

The patterns I would watch for are smooth hockey-stick growth with no capacity explanation, margins that improve every year without a reason, working capital that shrinks as sales grow, and a balance sheet that “balances” only because a plug sits in other current liabilities. Tools that auto-balance projections are convenient, but the plug figure is exactly where the judgement belongs.

Also be careful with any tool that writes credit notes or approval probabilities. A banker will form their own view; a document that oversells is more likely to lose trust than to win a sanction.

## Keep the working file

Keep the source documents, the assumption sheet, the tool’s output and your review notes together in the client file. If the bank asks how a figure was derived, or the account comes under stress later, you will want to show the basis rather than a screenshot of a tool. The same habit underpins my [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI prepare CMA data for a bank loan?

AI tools can extract financials, build the CMA forms, roll forward projections and compute ratios quickly. A CA still needs to tie the history to audited accounts, evidence every assumption and review the plug figures before the file goes to the bank.

### How do banks assess working capital for small businesses?

The RBI’s MSME FAQs say banks should appraise genuine requirements based on the business cycle, and that under the Nayak Committee approach limits for small units are computed at a minimum of 20% of estimated turnover for credit limits up to ₹5 crore.

### Is collateral needed for small MSE loans?

According to the RBI’s MSME FAQs, banks are mandated not to accept collateral security for loans up to ₹10 lakh to units in the MSE sector.

### What should a CA check in an AI-generated project report?

The tie-out of historical figures, the evidence for each projection assumption, consistency of working capital days, a manual DSCR check, the client’s current MSME classification and any claims in the narrative the client cannot support.

## Sources

- [RBI: FAQs on Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (updated 29 July 2025)](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/MICRO30072025E.pdf)
- [World Economic Forum with IndiaAI (MeitY) and the Office of the PSA: Transforming Small Businesses — An AI Playbook for India’s SMEs (August 2025)](https://www.psa.gov.in/CMS/web/sites/default/files/publication/WEF_Transforming_Small_Businesses_2025.pdf)
- [PIB: MSME investment and turnover limits enhanced 2.5 and 2 times (Union Budget 2025-26)](https://pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2098389)

# DPDP Act and AI in CA Firms in India: A Client-Data Decision Rubric

> How CA firms in India should use AI under the DPDP Act and Rules, 2025: decide your role, vendor terms, safeguards and logs, with a rubric and Monday checklist.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-dpdp-act-and-ai-in-ca-firms-in-india-a-client-data-decision-rubric
Last updated: 2026-10-19

CA insights · 2026-10-19 · 7 min read

How CA firms in India should use AI under the DPDP Act and Rules, 2025: decide your role, vendor terms, safeguards and logs, with a rubric and Monday checklist.

Key takeaways

- Under the DPDP Act, 2023, a CA firm can be a Data Fiduciary or a Data Processor depending on the engagement; decide which before any AI tool touches client personal data.
- Most operational obligations in the DPDP Rules, 2025, including security safeguards and breach intimation, commence eighteen months after the 13 November 2025 Gazette publication, in May 2027.
- Rule 6 safeguards read as an AI checklist: mask identifiers, use firm-managed accounts, keep logs for one year and put security terms in the processor contract.
- Breach intimation runs to affected individuals without delay and to the Data Protection Board, with a detailed report within seventy-two hours unless the Board allows longer.
- Score every client-data AI workflow on role clarity, minimisation, vendor terms, access, logs, data location, human review and breach readiness before it runs.

Most CA practices in India now have someone pasting client material into an AI assistant, and some of it is personal data: salary registers, Form 16s, KYC documents, director details for ROC filings. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 that is a question of responsibility, contract and safeguards, and the DPDP Rules, 2025 have now put dates on it. I write as Pratik Bajoria, Chartered Accountant, ex-Big 4 and founder of Findost. This is a partner’s decision rubric, not legal advice and not a tool review.

## Why the clock matters for CA firms now

The Rules were published in the Gazette on 13 November 2025 as G.S.R. 846(E) and commence in stages. Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 took effect on publication; Rule 4, on consent managers, follows a year later. The operational core — notice, security safeguards, breach intimation, retention and erasure, in Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 — commences eighteen months after publication, in May 2027. A client-data AI workflow started this quarter will still be running then, and designing for it now is cheaper than retrofitting habits across every associate’s laptop mid-season.

## First decide your role, engagement by engagement

The Act turns on two roles. A Data Fiduciary decides why and how personal data is processed; a Data Processor processes it on a fiduciary’s behalf. A CA firm can be either. Running payroll or bookkeeping for a company that decides what it collects about its staff and vendors, the firm may well be the client’s processor. Holding an individual’s documents to prepare and file their return, it may look more like a fiduciary. The classification turns on facts and engagement terms, so take counsel’s view; what matters here is the consequence.

A fiduciary stays responsible under section 8(1) for processing done on its behalf, irrespective of any agreement to the contrary, and section 8(2) allows it to involve a processor only under a valid contract. An AI vendor receiving client personal data sits in that chain. If the firm is itself the client’s processor, the client’s obligations flow down through the engagement letter, and an unapproved tool puts the client and the relationship at risk.

Alongside this sits Subsection 114 of [ICAI’s Code of Ethics](https://disc.icai.org/code-of-ethics/): no disclosure of client information outside the firm without proper and specific authority, and reasonable steps so that staff respect that duty. The DPDP Act adds statutory consequences to a duty the profession already had.

## What the Rules expect of safeguards, read as an AI checklist

Rule 6 lists the minimum “reasonable security safeguards”. Four matter most for AI:

- **Protect the data itself** by encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens: mask PANs, account numbers and names before a prompt whenever the task does not need them.
- **Control access** to the computer resources used: firm-managed business accounts, not personal logins.
- **Keep logs** with monitoring and review so unauthorised access can be detected and investigated, retained for one year unless another law requires otherwise.
- **Write security into the processor contract**, as the Rule expects.

Rule 7 adds breach intimation: affected individuals without delay, and the Data Protection Board without delay, with a detailed report within seventy-two hours unless the Board allows longer. The Government’s own explainer notes penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to maintain reasonable security safeguards and up to ₹200 crore for failing to notify a breach.

## A decision rubric for any AI workflow that touches client personal data

Score each workflow from one to five on every axis before it touches a live client file. A one on role clarity, vendor terms or human review means redesign before it runs. The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) groups this work as govern, map, measure and manage; treat the rubric as the “map” step for client data.

Evaluation framework only. Score your own workflows; this is not legal advice or benchmark data.

| Axis | Question to answer | Proceed (5) | Stop and redesign (1) | Your score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Role clarity | Fiduciary or processor on this engagement? | Recorded and reflected in the engagement letter | Never asked | \_\_\_ |
| Minimisation | Does the task need identifiers? | Masked or removed; only needed fields sent | Full ledgers or KYC pasted by default | \_\_\_ |
| Vendor terms | What do terms say on training, retention, sub-processors? | Business plan; terms read and filed by a partner | Consumer account; terms unread | \_\_\_ |
| Access | Who uses it, from which account? | Firm-managed accounts, multi-factor sign-in, leavers process | Personal logins or shared passwords | \_\_\_ |
| Logs and retention | Can we show who sent what, and delete on schedule? | Logs available; retention set against Rule 6 | No logs, or history kept on personal devices | \_\_\_ |
| Data location | Where is data processed and stored? | Region recorded; watch for section 16 notifications | Unknown | \_\_\_ |
| Human review | Who checks output before it leaves the firm? | Named reviewer, recorded sign-off | Output goes straight to the client | \_\_\_ |
| Breach readiness | Wrong file pasted: who is told, how fast? | Written escalation path; partner assesses within hours | Found at the next peer review | \_\_\_ |

Model quality does not appear. A modest tool on a firm-managed account, with masked inputs and a named reviewer, is easier to defend than a stronger one used from a personal login.

## Where AI still earns its place in the practice

None of this keeps AI out of the firm. Research on a provision, the structure of a reply, checklists and working-paper templates need no personal data; start there. Where client data is unavoidable, follow the pattern in [how Indian CA firms can use AI for GST reconciliation without risking client data](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-28-how-indian-ca-firms-can-use-ai-for-gst-reconciliation-without-risking-client-data). The [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india) sets review gates once a workflow is live; this rubric decides whether it may touch personal data at all. For the vendor choice, see [ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini for a CA firm in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-05-chatgpt-vs-copilot-vs-gemini-how-a-ca-firm-in-india-should-choose-an-ai-assistant), then read the vendor’s own documentation for your plan, such as [Microsoft’s Copilot privacy page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/microsoft-365-copilot-privacy) or [Google’s Workspace generative AI privacy hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/generative-ai/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub).

For the wider map, start at the [AI for chartered accountants in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india) hub. To score your own opportunities, take the free [AI Opportunity Scorecard](https://pratikbajoria.com/scorecard), see the scoped [AI Opportunity Audit](https://pratikbajoria.com/audit), or [book a discovery call](https://pratikbajoria.com/#contact).

## Monday-morning checklist

- List every AI tool in use, including personal accounts associates actually use.
- For your five busiest client-data workflows, record whether the firm is fiduciary or processor.
- Move client work to firm-managed business accounts.
- Write a one-line masking rule: no PAN, Aadhaar, account numbers or salary data in prompts unless needed and the tool is approved.
- Read each approved tool’s data terms; file the version and date.
- Ask counsel to review a data-processing clause and AI-use line for your engagement letter.
- Name the person who receives a suspected breach report, and rehearse the seventy-two-hour sequence once.
- Put May 2027 in the partners’ calendar and re-score live workflows each quarter.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does the DPDP Act apply to CA firms that use AI?

Yes, where the firm processes digital personal data such as salary records, KYC or individual tax files. It acts as a Data Fiduciary or a Data Processor depending on the engagement, and an AI vendor receiving that data normally becomes a processor in the chain.

### When do the DPDP Rules, 2025 obligations apply?

The Rules were published on 13 November 2025. Some took effect immediately; most operational obligations, including security safeguards and breach intimation, commence eighteen months later, in May 2027.

### Can a CA firm use ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini on client data?

Only after deciding its role for that data, reading the vendor’s business data terms, using firm-managed accounts, masking unneeded identifiers and naming a human reviewer.

# How to Use Claude or ChatGPT for GSTR-2B Reconciliation: A CA’s Method

> A CA’s step-by-step method for GSTR-2B reconciliation with Claude or ChatGPT: what to upload, the prompt structure, IMS actions and the checks before 3B.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-19-how-to-use-claude-or-chatgpt-for-gstr-2b-reconciliation-a-ca-s-method
Last updated: 2026-10-19

CA insights · 2026-10-19 · 4 min read

Most of what ranks today for “Claude AI for GST reconciliation” is a LinkedIn post with a copy-paste prompt, or a vendor page selling a tool. The prompts are not wrong. What they leave out is the part that decides whether the input tax credit you claim is defensible: what the law says GSTR-2B is for, what the Invoice Management System changes, and which matches a person must check before GSTR-3B goes in.

This is the method I would hand to a senior article assistant in a CA firm. It works with Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot, and it keeps the professional judgement where it belongs.

## Why GSTR-2B is the file that matters

Since 1 January 2022, after clause (aa) was inserted in section 16(2) of the CGST Act, input tax credit can be availed only to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B. CBIC set this out plainly in [Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-06/circular-cgst-193.pdf). So the reconciliation is not a nice-to-have report. It is the evidence that each rupee of credit in GSTR-3B is backed by a supplier filing.

That changes how you should use AI. The model is a fast matching assistant. It is not the authority on eligibility, blocked credits or time limits, and it should never be the last step before filing.

## Account for IMS before you reconcile

The [GSTN advisory on the Invoice Management System](https://tutorial.gst.gov.in/downloads/news/revised_advisory_on_ims.pdf) explains that a recipient can accept, reject or keep pending each invoice the supplier saves in GSTR-1, IFF or GSTR-1A. Invoices with no action are deemed accepted and move into GSTR-2B. A draft GSTR-2B is generated on the 14th of the following month, and if you act on invoices after that you need to recompute it before filing GSTR-3B.

In practice this means two passes. First, reconcile the purchase register against the IMS dashboard and decide accept, reject or pending. Second, reconcile against the final GSTR-2B you will actually rely on. Asking an AI tool to compare against a stale 2B download is the most common mistake I see.

## The step-by-step workflow

- Export the purchase register from Tally, Zoho Books or the client’s ERP as CSV, with supplier GSTIN, invoice number, invoice date, taxable value and each tax head in separate columns.
- Download GSTR-2B (and the IMS view, if you are still deciding actions) from the portal in Excel.
- Clean both files first: remove subtotal rows, standardise dates and strip spaces and prefixes from invoice numbers. Ask the model to do this as a separate step and to show you the rows it dropped.
- Ask for matching on GSTIN plus normalised invoice number first, then on GSTIN plus amount within a small tolerance, and keep the two result sets separate so you can see which matches were fuzzy.
- Request four output tables: exact matches, amount or date differences, in books but not in 2B, and in 2B but not in books.
- Have the model draft supplier follow-up emails for the missing items, but send them yourself.

## A prompt structure that holds up

Good prompts for this work are specific about columns, tolerances and outputs, and they forbid guessing. I write them in this order: describe each file and its columns; state the matching keys and the tolerance; list the output tables; and add two rules: “do not infer missing GSTINs” and “list every row you could not classify”.

Then test the prompt on a month you have already reconciled by hand. If the AI result differs from your manual working, find out why before you trust it on a live month. That one test teaches a team more about the tool’s limits than any training video.

## What must stay with the reviewer

- Eligibility: blocked credits, personal use and the other conditions in section 16 and section 17 are judgements, not matches.
- Fuzzy matches: anything matched on amount alone, or with a changed invoice number, needs a human look at the invoice.
- Rejections in IMS: rejecting an invoice affects the supplier too, so the decision should sit with someone who knows the commercial relationship.
- The final ITC figure in GSTR-3B: a partner or manager should tie it to the reconciliation and sign off.

## Data protection is part of the method

Purchase registers for proprietors and small firms often contain personal data. The [DPDP Rules, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014) were notified in November 2025 with a phased timeline, so now is the time to decide which AI accounts may receive client files. Use a business or enterprise plan with training on your data switched off, keep files in firm-controlled storage, and remove fields the matching does not need. My [AI controls checklist for CA firms](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-controls-checklist-ca-firms-india) has the wider list.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can Claude or ChatGPT do GSTR-2B reconciliation?

They can clean the files, match invoices on GSTIN, invoice number and amount, and produce exception tables quickly. They cannot decide eligibility or replace the reviewer’s sign-off on the ITC claimed in GSTR-3B.

### Why reconcile with GSTR-2B rather than GSTR-2A?

From 1 January 2022, section 16(2)(aa) of the CGST Act limits input tax credit to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B, as CBIC Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST confirms.

### How does IMS affect reconciliation?

Under IMS a recipient accepts, rejects or keeps invoices pending. Deemed-accepted and accepted invoices flow into GSTR-2B. If you act after the draft 2B is generated on the 14th, recompute GSTR-2B before filing GSTR-3B.

### Is it safe to upload client purchase registers to an AI tool?

Only to a firm-approved business account with training on your data switched off and retention settings you have checked. Remove fields the matching does not need, and record which tool processed which client file.

## Sources

- [CBIC Circular No. 193/05/2023-GST: ITC only up to the extent communicated in GSTR-2B from 1 January 2022 (section 16(2)(aa))](https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-06/circular-cgst-193.pdf)
- [GSTN: Advisory on the Invoice Management System (IMS) — accept, reject or keep pending before GSTR-2B](https://tutorial.gst.gov.in/downloads/news/revised_advisory_on_ims.pdf)
- [PIB: Government notifies DPDP Rules (14 November 2025)](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2190014)

# AI for CARO 2020 Reporting: Where It Helps and Where Judgement Stays

> CARO 2020 asks auditors for a statement on 21 clauses. A clause-by-clause guide to where AI can assemble the evidence, what the auditor must still decide, and how to document the tool.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-16-ai-for-caro-2020-reporting-where-it-helps-and-where-judgement-stays
Last updated: 2026-10-22

CA insights · 2026-10-16 · 8 min read

CARO reporting is a good test of where AI belongs in a statutory audit. Most clauses need the auditor to find, assemble and check specific evidence: title deeds, inventory verification results, loan terms, quarterly returns to banks, statutory dues, whistle-blower complaints. That is laborious and well suited to machines. Each clause then ends in a statement the auditor signs, and that part is not.

Having spent my early years on Big 4 audit files, I know how much of a CARO working is hunting for documents rather than thinking. This guide goes clause by clause: what the order asks, where a tool genuinely saves time, and where the auditor’s judgement has to stay in charge.

## What CARO 2020 asks for

The [Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?relid=199571) was issued on 25 February 2020 under section 143(11) of the Companies Act, 2013, replacing CARO 2016. Its start date was deferred twice; ICAI’s [announcement of 19 December 2020](https://icai.org/post/extension-applicability-date-caro-2020-for-one-year) confirms that, after the Ministry of Corporate Affairs order of 17 December 2020, it applies to financial years commencing on or after 1 April 2021. FY 2021-22 was therefore the first year reported under it, and this year’s audits are its fifth cycle.

- Discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate of each class of inventory found on physical verification.
- Whether quarterly returns or statements filed with banks agree with the books, where working capital limits above ₹5 crore were sanctioned on the security of current assets.
- A prescribed lender-wise format for defaults in repaying loans or interest, and whether the company is a declared wilful defaulter.
- Whether term loans were used for the purpose obtained, and details of any diversion.
- Cash losses in the current and preceding year, resignation of statutory auditors, and whistle-blower complaints considered by the auditor.

The [order’s text](https://taxguru.in/company-law/caro-2020.html) sets out the matters in paragraph 3 from clause (i) to clause (xxi), and it does not apply to reports on consolidated financial statements except for clause (xxi). The [press release](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?relid=199571) lists what was new, and most of it is data-heavy:

## Check applicability before anything else

The [order](https://taxguru.in/company-law/caro-2020.html) excludes banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 companies, one person companies and small companies. It also excludes a private company that is not a holding or subsidiary company of a public company, provided three limits are all met: paid-up capital and reserves and surplus of not more than ₹1 crore on the balance sheet date, borrowings from any bank or financial institution of not more than ₹1 crore at any point in the year, and total revenue of not more than ₹10 crore for the year.

Note the wording on borrowings: “at any point of time during the financial year”. A year-end balance of nil does not settle it. This is the first place I would use a tool, to scan the full year’s bank statements and loan ledgers for the peak balance, because a wrong applicability call makes everything after it wasted effort.

The small company test is defined in the Companies Act and its rules and has been revised over the years, so check the thresholds in force for the year under audit rather than relying on memory.

## Clause by clause: what AI can prepare and what you decide

The table below is how I would split the work on the most evidence-heavy clauses. The left-hand columns come from the [order](https://taxguru.in/company-law/caro-2020.html); the right-hand columns are my practice view, not a regulatory requirement.

CARO 2020: where a tool helps and where the auditor’s judgement decides. Clause references from the order; split of work is the author’s practice view.

| Clause | What the order asks | What AI can prepare | What the auditor decides |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Property, plant and equipment | Proper records, physical verification, title deeds held in the company’s name, revaluation, benami proceedings | Match the fixed asset register to title deeds and verification sheets; list mismatched names and missing deeds | Whether records are “proper” and whether title exceptions are reportable |
| (ii) Inventory and bank returns | Coverage of physical verification, 10% discrepancies by class, quarterly returns to banks vs books (limits above ₹5 crore) | Compute discrepancy by class; reconcile each quarterly stock statement to the books and list differences with amounts | Whether coverage was appropriate and whether a difference is a reportable non-agreement |
| (iii) Loans, guarantees and investments | Terms, repayment schedules, overdues, renewals and loans repayable on demand | Extract terms from agreements; build the repayment and overdue schedule | Whether terms are prejudicial to the company’s interest |
| (vii) Statutory dues | Regularity in depositing undisputed dues; arrears outstanding over six months; disputed dues by forum | Reconcile GST, PF, ESI and TDS challans to liabilities and due dates; age the arrears | Which items are disputed and how the forum is described |
| (ix) Borrowings | Defaults in the prescribed lender-wise format, wilful defaulter, diversion of term loans and short-term funds used long term | Compare sanction letters to actual repayments and fund flows; draft the default table | Whether funds were diverted and whether a default exists in substance |
| (xi) Fraud and whistle-blowing | Fraud noticed or reported, ADT-4 filings, whistle-blower complaints considered | Index minutes, complaint logs and legal correspondence so nothing is missed | Everything: read the sources in full, never a summary |
| (xvii) to (xix) Losses, auditor resignation, going concern | Cash losses, outgoing auditor’s concerns, material uncertainty on meeting liabilities within one year | Calculate cash losses; build the ratio, ageing and maturity analysis | Whether a material uncertainty exists |
| (xx) CSR | Unspent amounts transferred to a Schedule VII fund or unspent CSR account in time | Trace CSR spend and transfers to the dates in section 135(6) | Whether a project is “ongoing” |

## Where AI earns its place

These are the same capabilities Gartner’s [2025 survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) found finance teams already using most, such as knowledge management and anomaly detection, applied to an audit file. The time saved is real; the evidence still has to be checked.

- Building the clause-by-clause evidence index: for each clause, what evidence is needed, where it sits and whether it has been received.
- Comparing quarterly stock statements submitted to banks with the books, period by period, and listing every difference with its amount.
- Reading loan agreements and sanction letters to extract repayment schedules and stated purposes, then comparing them with actual repayments and utilisation.
- Summarising board minutes, whistle-blower logs and legal correspondence so the team knows what to read in full.
- Analysing inventory verification sheets by class to see which classes approach the 10% threshold.

## A worked routine for clause (ii)(b)

The bank return comparison is where I see the biggest saving, because it is pure matching. A routine that works: export the four quarterly stock and book-debt statements filed with each bank, export the trial balance and debtors and inventory ledgers at the same four dates, and ask the tool to produce one table per quarter with the bank figure, the book figure, the difference and the percentage.

The tool should then do nothing more. A person reads each difference, asks management why it arose, and decides whether it is a timing difference, a provisional figure later revised, or a genuine non-agreement that the order requires to be reported with details. The [ICAI Guidance Note on CARO 2020](https://cag.gov.in/uploads/media/Guidance-note-on-CARO-2020-064e84867178ba9-47322653.pdf) is the reference for how to word that reporting.

## Where judgement stays

Each clause ends in a statement: whether something is so, and if not, the details. Deciding whether a difference between a bank statement and the books is a reportable non-agreement, whether funds were diverted, or whether a material uncertainty exists about meeting liabilities falling due within a year requires professional judgement and knowledge of the client. AI can surface the facts; it cannot weigh them.

There is also a quieter risk: summaries that miss something. A model asked to summarise board minutes may drop the one line about a fraud investigation. I would never let a summary replace reading the source for clauses dealing with fraud, whistle-blower complaints or defaults.

## Document the tool like any other procedure

Internal audit now has a standard on this. ICAI’s [SIA 240](https://internalaudit.icai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Comp-of-Stnd-on-Internal-Audit-26.pdf) asks for tool use to be planned, outputs validated for completeness and accuracy, configurations and results documented, and professional judgement applied to all tool-based findings. Statutory auditors are bound by the SAs rather than the SIAs, but the discipline transfers well to a CARO file: record what the tool did, what was checked by a person, and what the conclusion rests on.

For the working-paper side of the same audit, see [AI for audit working papers in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-30-ai-for-audit-working-papers-in-india-what-a-ca-should-automate-and-what-must-stay-human). The same evidence often feeds the tax audit report too, which I cover in [AI for tax audit in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-09-ai-for-tax-audit-in-india-form-3cd-this-year-form-26-next-year). If you are training juniors to do this matching, [how CA firms should train article assistants now](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-15-ai-and-articleship-how-ca-firms-should-train-article-assistants-now) sets out a review-first approach, and the wider plan sits in the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india).

## A Monday checklist for the CARO file

Before the busy season starts, five things are worth agreeing as a team.

- Applicability decided and documented, with the peak-borrowing check done on the full year’s data.
- An evidence index with one line per clause and sub-clause, owner and status.
- A list of clauses where AI output may be used as a starting point, and those where it may not.
- A rule that every tool-generated schedule carries the source file names and the reviewer’s initials.
- Partner review of every clause that ends in an exception, against source documents rather than summaries.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many clauses does CARO 2020 have?

Paragraph 3 of CARO 2020 sets out matters from clause (i) to clause (xxi). Only clause (xxi) applies to the auditor’s report on consolidated financial statements.

### From which year does CARO 2020 apply?

After two deferrals, CARO 2020 applies to financial years commencing on or after 1 April 2021, so FY 2021-22 was the first year reported under it. CARO 2016 applied to FY 2020-21.

### Can AI prepare CARO reporting?

It can assemble and compare evidence for each clause, such as stock statements against books or loan terms against repayments. The statement made under each clause is the auditor’s judgement and must rest on evidence a person has checked.

### Which companies are exempt from CARO 2020?

Banking, insurance, section 8, one person and small companies, and private companies that are not a holding or subsidiary of a public company with paid-up capital and reserves and borrowings each of not more than ₹1 crore and total revenue of not more than ₹10 crore.

### What did CARO 2020 add on bank borrowings?

Where working capital limits above ₹5 crore were sanctioned on the security of current assets, the auditor reports whether the quarterly returns or statements filed with banks agree with the books, with details if they do not.

### Should AI summaries be used for the fraud clause?

No. Use a tool to index minutes and complaint logs so nothing is missed, but read the source documents in full for fraud, whistle-blower and default matters.

# AI and Articleship: How CA Firms Should Train Article Assistants Now

> Articleship is now two years, and AI drafts much of what articles used to learn on. A practical training plan for CA firms: review before preparation, manual fundamentals first, and clear tool rules.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-15-ai-and-articleship-how-ca-firms-should-train-article-assistants-now
Last updated: 2026-10-22

CA insights · 2026-10-15 · 7 min read

For most of us, articleship was where we learned the job by doing the repetitive parts: vouching, ticking, preparing schedules, chasing documents. A lot of that preparation can now be drafted by a tool in minutes. If firms keep training article assistants the old way, they will produce juniors who are good at work that is disappearing and untrained in the work that remains.

The time available has also shrunk. Under ICAI’s New Scheme of Education and Training, practical training is two years, so firms have less time to get it right. This is how I would redesign those two years, with the regulatory facts first and my practice view clearly marked as such.

## The training window under the new scheme

According to ICAI’s [FAQs on the New Scheme of Education and Training](https://resource.cdn.icai.org/75315bos-faqs-nset-july1.pdf), practical training starts after a student passes both groups of the Intermediate examination and completes the four-week ICITSS course, and lasts two years. Industrial training of 9 to 12 months is permitted in the last part of those two years, and 12 leaves are allowed in each year. The four-week Advanced ICITSS course comes after practical training and before the Final examination.

Two years, minus leave and exam preparation, is not much time to turn a student into someone a partner can rely on. That argues for being deliberate about what articles spend their hours on.

## The scheme in numbers

The figures below are all from ICAI’s own [FAQs](https://resource.cdn.icai.org/75315bos-faqs-nset-july1.pdf). They matter for planning because they fix how much of a student’s time is actually available to the firm.

Key timings under ICAI’s New Scheme of Education and Training. Source: ICAI Board of Studies FAQs.

| Item | What the scheme says | Why it matters to the firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start of practical training | After passing both Intermediate groups and completing four-week ICITSS | Articles arrive with basic IT and soft-skills training already done |
| Duration | Two years | Plan the curriculum in quarters, not as an open-ended apprenticeship |
| Leave | 12 leaves in each year | Roughly 24 days across the term; schedule the manual fundamentals early |
| Industrial training | 9 to 12 months, in the last part of the two years | Some articles leave for industry before the busy season you planned around |
| Final exam eligibility | Practical training completed six months before the first day of the exam month | Expect exam leave and reduced availability late in the term |
| Advanced ICITSS | Four weeks, after practical training, before the Final | Not part of the firm’s two years |
| Self-paced online modules | Four sets (A to D); pass mark 50% per module | SET D includes Digital Ecosystem and Controls, a natural link to firm tool policies |

## The profession is already moving

ICAI has been unusually quick on AI. At its [AI Innovation Summit 2026](https://www.icai.org/post/icai-ais2026-26062026), the Institute said it had trained over 50,000 members in AI and developed more than 150 GPT-based tools, and it launched Level 3 of its AI certificate course for members. Students have their own tools too: ICAI’s [November 2024 release](https://icai.org/post/prc-icai-unveils-groundbreaking-ca-gpt-platform) reported a GPT for CA students covering Foundation, Intermediate and Final, with over 50,000 students using it at the time.

So articles will arrive already using AI. The firm’s job is not to introduce the tools; it is to teach professional habits around them.

## Teach review before preparation

The most valuable skill a junior can build now is checking machine output against evidence. I would restructure the first months of articleship around that.

- Give articles AI-drafted schedules with deliberate errors planted, and assess how many they find and how they prove each one.
- Make “show me the source document” the default response to any number an article presents, whoever or whatever produced it.
- Have articles write the review note on an AI draft, not just correct it, so the reasoning is visible.
- Rotate them through exception handling: the items a reconciliation tool could not match are where judgement is learned.

## Keep the fundamentals manual for a while

There is a real risk of juniors who can operate a tool but cannot do the underlying work. I would keep a short period of fully manual work on core tasks, such as a bank reconciliation, a GST return working and a set of audit vouching, before introducing AI on the same task. You cannot review what you have never done.

The internal audit standards make a similar point for the whole team. ICAI’s [SIA 240 on use of tools](https://internalaudit.icai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Comp-of-Stnd-on-Internal-Audit-26.pdf) requires that the team has the competencies to use selected tools and that the engagement lead ensures periodic training as tools evolve. The same principle applies in any practice.

## A two-year plan, quarter by quarter

This is the structure I would use. It is a practice suggestion, not an ICAI requirement, and it assumes a mixed audit and tax practice.

- Quarter 1: manual fundamentals. Bank reconciliation, vouching, a GST return working and a TDS working done by hand, reviewed line by line.
- Quarter 2: review of machine output. The same tasks, now with AI-drafted versions containing planted errors; the article writes the review note.
- Quarters 3 and 4: evidence-heavy audit work, such as the clause-by-clause evidence index for CARO and the tax audit report, where tools prepare and articles check.
- Quarters 5 and 6: exception handling and client conversations. Unmatched items, notice replies and queries to management, with a senior present.
- Quarters 7 and 8: mentoring juniors and, for those leaving for industrial training, a handover file that shows their review notes.

## What to teach on real engagements

Two engagement types work especially well for this. In statutory audit, CARO reporting is mostly evidence assembly followed by a judgement, which makes it ideal for teaching the line between the two; I walk through it clause by clause in [AI for CARO 2020 reporting](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-16-ai-for-caro-2020-reporting-where-it-helps-and-where-judgement-stays). For working papers generally, [AI for audit working papers in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-30-ai-for-audit-working-papers-in-india-what-a-ca-should-automate-and-what-must-stay-human) covers what SA 230 still demands of the file whoever drafted it.

On the tax side, [AI for tax audit in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-09-ai-for-tax-audit-in-india-form-3cd-this-year-form-26-next-year) is a good second-year assignment: lots of data matching, and a clear point where a CA has to sign. If articles move faster because of tools, the firm also has to think about how that shows up in fees, which I discuss in [how CA firms should price work when AI cuts the hours](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-14-how-ca-firms-in-india-should-price-work-when-ai-cuts-the-hours).

## Rules articles should know on day one

None of this needs a large programme. A one-page policy, a planted-error exercise in the first month, and partners who ask “how do you know?” consistently will do more than any course. If you are weighing formal courses for the team, I compared the options in [AI courses for chartered accountants in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-ai-courses-for-chartered-accountants-in-india-what-is-worth-it). For the firm-wide plan, start from the [AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-in-india).

- Which AI tools are approved, and that client data never goes into personal accounts.
- What may be drafted by AI, and what must be done or concluded by a person.
- That every AI-assisted output is labelled as such in the file until reviewed.
- Who to ask when an AI answer and their own work disagree, and that disagreement is worth raising.

## How to tell whether it is working

Measure the habit, not the tool. At the end of each quarter I would look at three things for every article: the share of planted errors they found, whether their review notes cite a source document for each point, and how many exceptions they escalated rather than cleared on their own. If those numbers improve, the training is working, whatever tools they used along the way.

A firm that wants to try this formally can treat the first cohort as a pilot, with a baseline and a go or stop decision at the end, using the approach in [how to run a 90-day AI pilot in a CA firm](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india).

## Frequently asked questions

### How long is CA articleship now?

Under ICAI’s New Scheme of Education and Training, practical training is two years, started after passing both groups of the Intermediate examination and completing ICITSS. Industrial training of 9 to 12 months is permitted in the last part.

### How many leaves are allowed during articleship?

ICAI’s FAQs on the new scheme allow 12 leaves in each year of the two-year practical training.

### Should article assistants use AI?

Yes, within firm rules on approved tools and client data, and after they have done the core tasks manually at least once. The priority is teaching them to review AI output against evidence.

### What AI training does ICAI offer?

ICAI runs an AI certificate course for members, with Level 3 launched at its AI Innovation Summit 2026, and provides CA GPT tools for members and students. It reported training over 50,000 members in AI by June 2026.

### What skills matter most for juniors now?

Checking outputs against source documents, writing clear review notes, handling exceptions and knowing when to escalate. Preparation still matters, but review is where trust is built.

### When can a student sit the CA Final under the new scheme?

According to ICAI’s FAQs, after registering for the Final, completing practical training six months before the first day of the exam month, completing Advanced ICITSS and qualifying all four self-paced online modules.

# How CA Firms in India Should Price Work When AI Cuts the Hours

> If AI halves preparation time, hourly billing hands the gain to the client. How Indian CA firms can price scope and risk instead, within ICAI’s rules on fees.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-14-how-ca-firms-in-india-should-price-work-when-ai-cuts-the-hours
Last updated: 2026-10-22

CA insights · 2026-10-14 · 4 min read

Every partner I speak to about AI eventually asks the same uncomfortable question: if this saves my team hours, and I bill by the hour or by a rate card built on hours, have I just cut my own fees?

Possibly. But only if pricing stays where it is. The more useful question is what the client is actually paying for, and whether that has changed. In most compliance and advisory work it has not: they are paying for a correct deliverable, delivered on time, with a professional standing behind it.

## How much time are we talking about?

Nobody has a reliable India-specific number for CA practices yet, and I would be wary of anyone who quotes one. The broader surveys give a sense of direction. Thomson Reuters’ [2025 Future of Professionals report](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/the-ai-adoption-reality-check-firms-with-ai-strategies-are-twice-as-likely-to-see-ai-driven-revenue-growth-those-without-risk-falling-behind-302490973.html), based on 2,275 professionals across legal, tax, accounting, audit, risk and trade, found respondents expecting AI to save five hours a week within a year. The same report found only 22% saying their organisation had a visible, defined AI strategy.

In India, Microsoft’s [2025 Work Trend Index findings](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2025/08/20/indias-workforce-goes-ai-first-as-frontier-firms-lead-the-transformation-microsoft-work-trend-index-2025/) reported that 93% of leaders intend to use AI agents to extend workforce capacity in the next 12 to 18 months. Clients will read the same headlines. Expect them to ask why the fee has not moved.

## First, know what you are not allowed to do

The obvious answer, "charge for the outcome", runs into the profession’s own rules. Under Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, read with [Regulation 192](https://icai.org/post/5645), a CA in practice may not charge fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the work, apart from specific exceptions such as receivers and liquidators, co-operative society audits and valuers for direct taxes. ICAI’s FAQs also say fees cannot be charged as a percentage of turnover except as Regulation 192 allows.

So for audit, tax and most compliance work, "value pricing" in an Indian practice means pricing the scope, the complexity and the risk of the engagement as a fixed fee agreed upfront, not tying the fee to a result.

## Price the deliverable, not the hours behind it

A fixed fee per deliverable lets the firm keep the efficiency it earns. The client gets certainty and a defined scope; the firm gets the benefit of doing the work faster. That only works if the scope is written down clearly, which is why I would revisit engagement letters at the same time. [SA 210’s illustrative engagement letters](https://www.icai.org/post/aasb-illustrative-audit-engagement-letter-under-companies-act-2013-17-12-2014) already provide for fees and billing arrangements to be agreed in writing; extend the same discipline to non-audit work.

- Define the deliverable: which returns, which reconciliations, which reports, by when.
- Define what is out of scope and how it will be priced, such as notices, revisions and additional entities.
- State what the client must provide and by when; late or messy data is the biggest driver of hours.
- Separate the review and sign-off component, which does not shrink with AI, from preparation, which does.

## What does not get cheaper

Review time, professional judgement and liability do not fall with AI. If anything, review becomes more important, because more of the first draft is produced by a tool. I would make that visible in proposals: a smaller preparation line, an unchanged review and sign-off line, and new lines for work that AI makes possible, such as monthly exception reports or faster turnaround on queries.

## Where the time saved should go

If the hours saved simply disappear into lower bills, the firm has funded the tools and given away the benefit. Decide before you roll AI out where the time will be redeployed, and measure it during a [time-boxed pilot](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india) rather than guessing.

- Into review quality: more time for the manager and partner on the judgement areas.
- Into new recurring services clients will pay for, such as monthly MIS or compliance health checks.
- Into capacity, so the firm can take on more clients in peak season without lowering standards.
- Into training, so article assistants and juniors learn to review machine output, not just prepare.

Faster preparation changes how juniors learn as well as what clients pay; I cover that in [AI and articleship](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-15-ai-and-articleship-how-ca-firms-should-train-article-assistants-now). For an example of work where the evidence is cheaper to assemble but the judgement is not, see [AI for CARO 2020 reporting](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-16-ai-for-caro-2020-reporting-where-it-helps-and-where-judgement-stays) and [AI for audit working papers in India](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-09-30-ai-for-audit-working-papers-in-india-what-a-ca-should-automate-and-what-must-stay-human).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a CA firm charge fees based on results?

Generally no. Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act and Regulation 192 prohibit fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent on findings or results, subject to specific exceptions such as receivers, liquidators, co-operative society audits and valuers for direct taxes.

### Should a CA firm reduce fees because it uses AI?

Not automatically. Clients pay for a correct, timely deliverable with professional responsibility behind it. A fixed fee for a clearly defined scope lets the firm keep efficiency gains while giving the client certainty.

### How much time does AI save accountants?

There is no reliable India-specific figure yet. In Thomson Reuters’ 2025 Future of Professionals survey of 2,275 professionals, respondents expected AI to save five hours a week within the next year.

### What should change in proposals?

Separate preparation from review and sign-off, define scope and exclusions precisely, and price new AI-enabled services, such as monthly exception reporting, as their own line.

# Using AI for TDS Reconciliation in Indian CA Firms: From 26AS to Form 168

> Form 26AS is now Form 168 under the new Act. How to automate TDS matching and the mismatch list, while a reviewer decides what to chase with the deductor.

Canonical: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-13-using-ai-for-tds-reconciliation-in-indian-ca-firms-from-26as-to-form-168
Last updated: 2026-10-22

CA insights · 2026-10-13 · 4 min read

TDS reconciliation is one of the least glamorous and most useful places to put AI in a practice. The volume is high, the rules are clear, and the cost of a missed mismatch is a demand, a refund delay or an uncomfortable call with the client.

It is also changing names. Under the [Income-tax Act, 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2248005), the statement many of us still call 26AS is [Form No. 168, the Annual Information Statement](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs), issued under section 510 read with Rule 245. The work behind it has not changed: match what the client booked with what others reported, and chase the differences.

## What the statement now contains

The Department’s [Form 168 FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs) describe two parts. Part A carries general information about the taxpayer. Part B carries TDS and TCS information, Statement of Financial Transactions data from reporting entities, payment of taxes, demands and refunds, and other information such as dividends, interest on refunds, and securities and mutual fund transactions. The Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS) aggregates this by category and is updated after feedback is processed.

In practice a reconciliation now has two jobs: tie the TDS credits the client is claiming to what deductors reported, and make sure the income behind those credits is fully reflected in the books and the return.

## What to automate

None of this needs a clever model. A well-written script does most of it, and an AI assistant is useful for writing and maintaining that script, for reading messy ledger narrations and for drafting the deductor emails. Gartner’s [2025 AI in Finance survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-18-gartner-survey-shows-finance-ai-adoption-remains-steady-in-2025) found error and anomaly detection among the three most common finance AI use cases; TDS matching is a very practical version of it.

- Parsing the downloaded statement into a clean table by deductor TAN, section, date and amount.
- Matching each entry to the client’s ledger, first exactly, then within tolerances on date and amount, with every fuzzy match labelled as such.
- Producing a mismatch list in three buckets: in the statement but not in the books, in the books but not in the statement, and in both with different amounts.
- Drafting the email to each deductor listing the missing or short-reported entries, with invoice references attached.
- Tracking responses and re-running the match after deductors file corrections.

## What a reviewer still decides

Whether a difference is a timing issue, a deductor error, a booking error or income the client has not recognised is a judgement. So is the decision to submit feedback on an AIS entry, to wait for a correction statement, or to report income that does not appear in the statement at all. The [FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-168-faqs) are explicit that actual income must be reported even if it is missing from the AIS, and that the TIS cannot be edited directly.

I would also keep a person on any match the tool marks as fuzzy. Fuzzy matching is where reconciliations quietly go wrong: two invoices of similar value from the same customer can be paired incorrectly, and the error will not surface until a deductor’s correction breaks it.

## The tax auditor will ask the deductor-side question too

For clients who deduct tax, the new tax audit report raises the bar. [Form 26](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-26-faqs) asks the auditor for the total number of transactions reported and not reported in the TDS/TCS return as it stands after the latest correction statement, and the amount of transactions not reported. A firm that already runs transaction-level matching for its clients’ own credits can extend the same scripts to their deduction compliance.

## A simple monthly rhythm

If this is the firm’s first AI workflow, run it as a time-boxed pilot with a baseline, as in my [90-day pilot playbook](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-how-to-run-a-90-day-ai-pilot-in-a-ca-firm-in-india).

- Download the statement and the ledger extract on a fixed day each month or quarter.
- Run the match and publish the three-bucket mismatch list to the reviewer.
- Reviewer classifies each item and approves the deductor emails.
- Re-run after corrections, and close items with a note of how they were resolved.
- Before the return, reconcile income heads in the TIS to the books and document every difference.

TDS matching is also a good early exercise for article assistants; see [AI and articleship](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-15-ai-and-articleship-how-ca-firms-should-train-article-assistants-now). For the statutory dues clause in the companies audit report, see [AI for CARO 2020 reporting](https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-16-ai-for-caro-2020-reporting-where-it-helps-and-where-judgement-stays).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Form 26AS still available?

Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026, the Annual Information Statement is Form No. 168, corresponding to Form 26AS and section 285BB under the 1961 Act.

### Can AI reconcile TDS automatically?

It can do the parsing, matching and drafting at high volume. A reviewer should still classify each difference, approve deductor follow-ups and decide on AIS feedback, and any fuzzy match should be confirmed by a person.

### What if income is missing from the AIS?

According to the Department’s FAQs, all actual income must be reported in the return even if it does not appear in the AIS.

### What does Form 26 ask about TDS returns?

For assessees who deduct or collect tax, the auditor reports the number of transactions reported and not reported in the TDS/TCS return after the latest correction, and the amount of transactions not reported.

## Sources

- [Income Tax Department: Form No. 26 FAQs (tax audit under section 63, Income-tax Act, 2025)](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/form-26-faqs)
